#1022. Tech Report: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1049 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games.
  • By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been.
  • And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma.

By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

In a recent development, on Friday, Dortmund had revealed a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Industry observers note that dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer noted. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”.

Sources indicate that “Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”.

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

It has been revealed that it goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

Industry observers note that what are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

Industry observers note that the latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

Sources indicate that it feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

According to recent reports, the latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Kenny Dalglish on his introduction to football in Glasgow

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During his 22-year playing career, Kenny Dalglish became one of the greatest players in British football history.

After winning no less than four Scottish titles and another four Scottish Cups with Celtic, Dalglish made the move south of the border in 1977, where his achievements with Liverpool outstripped even those he accomplished at Celtic Park.

But it was in Glasgow where the foundations of this great career were laid, from Sunday morning kickabouts and makeshift goalposts and onto amatuer football and apprenticeships.

“My dad took me to the football when I was a wee boy, so I started to get into it and we had a bit of grass in the back garden, six-by-six – after the game, I'd go back and have a kickabout there with my dad,” Dalglish reminises to FourFourTwo. “He was a Rangers fan, so he took me there – my first hero was a player that no-one would have heard of now, a centre-forward named Don Kitchenbrand. I thought, ‘He must be good, he scores goals all the time!'.

While Dalglish would end his career with almost 350 goals, he started further back on the pitch.

“When I was seven, I played as a goalkeeper before moving outfield – one of the boys' dads must have been a plumber, because they used to get these wee poles and fit posts onto a crossbar, then got nets from somewhere,” he continues.

“That was our wee team on a Sunday. “Why did I become a good player? I never thought I was that good – it was for other people to think that. A lot of people help you on the way – the most key person is the one who starts you off, and that was my dad. I'd play for school on a Saturday morning, then my amateur club in the afternoon. Mum was there too – there was never enough money, so if there was a tear in a sock, the mothers were there with a knitting needle. They took turns washing the strips as well. It was really communal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sources indicate that “When I was 14, we moved to high-rise flats near Ibrox. I was about to leave school – you left at 15 then – and I'd been playing football with the school, as well as an amateur club, Possil YM. I got into the Glasgow Schools under-13s, under-14s and under-15s teams – I could have gone to a latest school near the flats we moved to, but thought, ‘I've been to my school since I was young, I don't want another one to get the credit.'.

“It was only right that the school where I was educated – supposedly! – was where I got into the Scottish squad. “The guy who took the Glasgow team was very prominent with the Scottish schoolboys – they got beat once, so he mentioned, ‘This boy could come and play.'.

“Then when you're leaving school, they put a piece of paper in front of you and say, ‘Get yourself a job.' That was a very limited choice for me, but my first job was as a van boy, delivering school books – they were educational books, but I never read any of them!

Recent findings suggest that “At my amateur club Glasgow United, we had a really good team and you could join a professional club at 15 as an apprentice, but I thought it would be more advantageous to try to get a trade instead. At a club, all you were doing in the summer was painting the crossbar or the terraces, doing something to help the groundsman.

It has been revealed that “I thought it would be a good idea to have a trade, so I got a job as an apprentice joiner. At that point, I was training twice a week with a semi-professional team, Cumbernauld United, but if I wasn't going to be a footballer, at least I'd have had something to fall back on.

According to recent reports, “I’d be a tradesman. It's just as well as football worked out for me, because I wasn't much cop with a saw and chisel…”.

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

Nike is set to replace Adidas as the official match ball provider for the Champions League and all other Uefa men’s club competitions from 2027.

The deal, which runs until 2031, was revealed on Monday, bringing an end to Adidas’ long-running association with the Champions League.

Nike will provide the official match balls for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League - marking the first time all three tournaments will have the same supplier - as well as ⁠the Super Cup, Uefa Youth League and ​Uefa ⁠Futsal Champions League.

The deal was unveiled by UC3, the commercial joint venture between UEFA and European Football Clubs (EFC), which debuted the tender process in March, and its agency Relevent Football Partners.

The Athletic reported that the deal is worth around $45m per year.

Nike Football vice president and general manager said: “We are excited and honoured to return to the Uefa Champions ‌League, one of football's biggest stages, after more ‌than two decades, and to bring Nike match balls across Uefa’s men's club competitions.

Industry observers note that “Football is the ⁠world's game, and the ball is at the centre of it, the one thing every player, in every competition, has in common. This is a long-term commitment for Nike.

“We will listen to the athlete's voice, push the edges of innovation, honour the prestige and tradition of these competitions, and make sure the ball represents the instinct, creativity and joy football brings ‌to billions of fans.”.

Analysts had remarked the deal would boost Nike's ​visibility but was unlikely to address the company's underlying challenges, ‌including slowing sales and a lag ⁠in product innovation that have stymied the sportswear giant in recent ⁠years.

“In terms of getting its groove back, high-visibility corporate partnerships are not the silver bullet,” ‌Zacks Investment Research analyst ​David Bartosiak had remarked.

“Whether you're reinventing ‌the wheel or reinventing the ball, ​you're still not bringing any sort of meaningful innovation.”.

#1012. How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League.
  • According to recent reports, I felt unbelievably ponderous.
  • In a recent development, not my words.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League.

According to recent reports, I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

In a recent development, not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

It has been revealed that this passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

It has been revealed that now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

Recent findings suggest that there have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”.

It has been revealed that football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have stated, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Recent findings suggest that again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

In a recent development, the first matter is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

It has been revealed that and maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

According to recent reports, if you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary matter derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

According to recent reports, what are the consequences of this newly introduced fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

Industry observers note that and here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to complications of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

According to recent reports, there are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest matter here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been stated out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.

For many, Peter Schmeichel was the greatest goalkeeper of his generation.

The Dane enjoyed a trophy-laden career with Manchester United and also played a huge part in helping his country to a remarkable European Championship victory in 1992.

It has been revealed that schmeichel would eventually be succeeded as Denmark’s No. 1 by Thomas Sorensen, with the former Sunderland stopper able able to benefit from training alongside his legendary compatriot.

“There was nothing better than watching him train,” Sorensen tells FourFourTwo. “It was great because you could see him firsthand and get a lot of experience.

There were times, however, when Schmeichel’s formidable reputation came to the fore at training.

Recent findings suggest that “It was also pretty intimidating,” Sorensen adds. “He could be quite rough sometimes. He’d put me in my place. One day he’d be my best friend and the next he wouldn’t even say, ‘Good morning’ to me.”.

But as the pair have got old, this relationship has mellowed.

“He was a strange character in some ways, but I’ve gotten to know him a lot better over the years and I’m still good friends with his son Kasper,” he adds. “He’s totally different now than he was in his playing days.”.

Schmeichel called time on his international career in 2001, leaving Sorensen with the somewhat tough task of replacing an all-time great in the Danish team.

“It wasn’t just me – there were a few of us dubbed ‘The next Peter Schmeichel’,” Sorensen recalls.

It has been revealed that “I ended up being the winning horse. From the outset, I knew I was different from him and wanted to do it my way. He was very loud, outspoken and aggressive on the pitch. I was a little bit calmer.

“I came in at the right time because I’ve spoken to a lot of goalkeepers who were in his shadow for years and never got the chance. It probably wasn’t as hard as people think. We had success as a team and I played some good games. That always helps.

“He wasn’t forgotten, but that changeover was accepted pretty rapidly.”.

Why James Trafford must now be England’s No 1

  • England outclassed Spain for an hour and then produced a backs-to-the-wall display for the final 30 minutes to cling on for a famous 3-2 triumph – their first ever away victory over a team ranked No 1 in the world and a first win over Spain in Madrid since 1987.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Industry observers note that as auditions go, it could hardly have been better. James Trafford was given the opportunity to show that he genuinely belongs in the England No 1 conversation by facing the world champions in their own back yard and he excelled.

England outclassed Spain for an hour and then produced a backs-to-the-wall display for the final 30 minutes to cling on for a famous 3-2 triumph – their first ever away victory over a team ranked No 1 in the world and a first win over Spain in Madrid since 1987. In other words, historic, and the defining memory of the clash will be Trafford’s remarkable double save in injury time to preserve the narrow advantage.

Industry observers note that the 24-year-old brilliantly repelled Fermin Lopez’s effort before recovering almost instantly to get across and somehow tip Aymeric Laporte’s rebound past the post. He was mobbed by teammates and while no England stop will ever have the same resonance of Gordon Banks’ almost mythical save from Pele at the 1970 World Cup, this immediately enters the tier just below.

He made six saves in total throughout the game – a number only bettered three times by England goalkeepers in the past 15 years according to WhoScored – and even in a first half where he had little shot-stopping to do, looked supremely comfortable on the ball and was accurate in his distribution. He was vital in beating the energetic Spanish press.

Leeds United paid a record £45m fee for a British goalkeeper to prise him away from Manchester City this summer and that is already looking like a snip. He has the highest save percentage in the Premier League this year (82.2 per cent according to FBRef ), while only the league’s top two sides, Arsenal and Brighton, have conceded fewer than the Whites’ eight goals. Trafford has been a key part of a Leeds defence that is suddenly one of the meanest around and has enabled Daniel Farke’s men to establish themselves in the top half of the table.

A penny for Enzo Maresca’s true thoughts. Given Gianluigi Donnarumma’s inconsistent form this season, there’s a strong argument that City jettisoned the wrong goalkeeper this summer and that the Englishman – who is not only better with the ball at his feet but also three years younger than the Italian – will prove to be the superior player. Perhaps he is already.

Industry observers note that in his four previous England caps, starting with his debut against Uruguay at Wembley back in March, he looked at ease, only really leaving the question of whether he could perform under pressure against the very, very best in the world and his display in Madrid answered that emphatically. Tournament football is another level entirely but at this point, it would be foolish to bet against Trafford stepping up and delivering on that stage as he has done at every other.

Which is why it’s now time for him to be anointed as England’s No 1 as they build towards Euro 2028. This is not to disparage Jordan Pickford, who has performed remarkably for England and continues to be a top-level goalkeeper but the upside play at this point is Trafford. The Three Lions have consistently fallen agonisingly short of getting over the line in major tournaments and, to be clear, Pickford holds zero blame for that fact, but the pursuit of such an elusive goal requires brave decisions to improve the fine margins and officially elevating Trafford qualifies.

Thomas Tuchel has already begun the process by splitting starts equally between previously undisputed No 1 Pickford and pretender Trafford over the past two international breaks. It’s notable that the more inexperienced man has been given the two assignments against world champions Spain. He could have been in goal for the more routine clash with Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, with Pickford between the sticks in Madrid, but instead Tuchel rightly decided he would learn more by Trafford entering the Metropolitano cauldron – and his man emerged without even being singed.

It has been revealed that the German was non-committal when asked post-match whether he now has a new first choice. “There’s no number one,” insisted Tuchel. “It’s a good double save [at the end]. That’s what we wanted. He had a brilliant match. It only works if you’re top from number one to 11.”.

It has been revealed that but the England boss will quietly be thrilled with the selection headache he now has and it does feel like a changing of the guard is slowly occurring. It may be harsh on Pickford, who has been generally underrated during his tenure as Three Lions No 1, but elite sport is a necessarily emotionless arena.

Pickford has been consistently outstanding since his international debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017, with Opta stats claiming he has made only two errors leading to goals in 94 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74 percent save ratio. He has made 33 appearances at major tournaments and been an integral part of England’s most sustained period of competitiveness (two world Cup semi-finals, two Euros finals) in their history.

Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya (39) has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford (27) at Everton and even this year, he is in a creditable sixth spot with a 73.7 save percentage in the Premier League.

Industry observers note that he has never made a glaring mistake that has cost England in a massive game but, under the radar, he had a slightly rocky World Cup this summer. Martin Baturina’s shot slipped through his hands for Croatia’s first of two goals and in the last-32 win over DR Congo, the 32-year-old was beaten too easily at his near post by Brian Cipenga’s shot for their opening goal. He was fortunate not to be sent off against Ghana when he ill-advisedly came off his line and clattered Prince Adu outside of the box.

Television cameras also caught Pickford in an animated conversation with Tuchel after a botched clearance at one point, with the goalkeeper giving as good as he got before his manager ended the discussion by shouting “do as I told you!”.

According to recent reports, throughout his England career, Pickford’s distribution has been decent, although sometimes patchy and Trafford presents a clear step up in that department. Purely in terms of physicality, the younger man’s 6ft 6in frame somewhat dwarfs the 6ft 1in Everton star. He has surpassed his rival in a number of ways.

It has been revealed that pickford should go down as one of England’s greatest goalkeepers – even if there is a somewhat surprising hesitance from many to bestow him with that honour – and he will deservedly clear 100 caps. But the time has come for James Trafford to be crowned as No 1. He’s earned it.

#1004. Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (866 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body.
  • The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally.
  • Recent findings suggest that that would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body.

The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already revealed that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times.

Recent findings suggest that that would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m.

Which is to say that Fifa, and by extension its all-controlling president Gianni Infantino, was right.

Wrong, mind you, about what it believes anybody with a modicum of taste would think is cool and enjoyable. Like putting Robbie Williams in everything; or cramming Madonna, and BTS, and Shakira, and Justin Bieber, and Ted Lasso, and the Muppets into a World Cup final half-time show that catered to the appetites of the lobotomized; or setting up a pre-final speech on greatness by Tom Cruise.

Wrong, too, about mandatory hydration breaks, and suspending red cards, and stretching the aforementioned, accursed half-time show to 27 minutes in violation of Fifa’s own rules.

Sources indicate that but right about all the things Fifa cares about. Which can be neatly reduced to money.

Right that exposing ticket sales – and even parking – to dynamic pricing, driving their prices far out of reach of your average fan, would pay off. Right that it could annex the secondary ticket market and take a hefty cut of resales. Right that the PR hit of cozying up to Donald Trump – who was already deeply unpopular, especially among America’s left-leaning soccer crowd – would not be mortal and, in fact, would not even cost Fifa any money at all. That tolerating the excesses of the Trump government – the disgraceful treatment of the Iranian team, its bluster about potential ICE action around stadiums and its denial of visas to fans and journalists hoping to attend the tournament – would be worth it in order to safeguard the money gusher. (These things may all yet be investigated, among about a million other things, but Fifa’s money is made all the same.).

It has been revealed that right, in the end, that the World Cup is too significant to fail. That the decadence and cravenness of the World Cup’s organizers will, in the end, be redeemed by the tournament itself. That the World Cup is unfuckupable.

As things stand, it looks like Infantino may very well survive the fallout of his foolhardy and utterly tone-deaf attempt to quickly and unilaterally sell a chunk of the World Cup’s commercial rights to private equity. That was a bridge too far even in the world’s most cynical sport, but the tournament’s profits appear to have consolidated his power in spite of it all. Infantino has an election to get through in March, but a great many of his ardent supporters are apparently unmoved by the scandal and stand resolutely behind him. While he can’t quite do whatever he wants, it appears he also can’t commit an act grievous enough to be dislodged from power.

As Fifa pointed out to the Athletic, the World Cup’s attendance of 6.8 million was unprecedented – the previous record, from the 1994 World Cup in the United States, was just under 3.6 million. And hat means bigger payouts for Fifa’s 211 member associations, each of which has a presidential-election vote.

Recent findings suggest that this, and only this, is why there is no reforming Fifa until the money stream is somehow slowed. The real power in soccer lies with the money – everything and everyone else is just a figurehead. The sport is organized and optimized to facilitate only the flow of money. We were reminded of this same truth just last week when comments emerged of Kylian Mbappé making light of a meme involving himself and China’s former leader Mao Zedong. The Real Madrid star swiftly lost several endorsement deals in China, and scurried to apologize faster than he’s ever loped after a through ball.

Sources indicate that infantino understands this innately and behaves accordingly. And for all his blundering behavior, for all the ugliness and moral insolvency of his grubby masterpiece, the final takeaway from the 2026 World Cup is that, actually, this is all fine. It worked. Pandering to politicians? Proof, meet pudding. The money poured in at an unprecedented flow rate, a rapids of revenue. So, you know, carry on.

And that, to use a term from these lands that have made Fifa even wealthier, sucks.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Heimir Hallgrimsson has been dealt a blow with captain Nathan Collins ruled out of the Republic of Ireland’s must-win Nations League clash with Kosovo.

The centre-back has returned to Brentford and will be replaced by Jimmy Dunne in the squad for the Republic’s final meeting of Group B3, where a win would secure them second place and a promotion play-off berth.

Collins missed the last international window with a calf glitch and felt discomfort in his knee late in Saturday’s 1-0 loss to group winners Austria.

“He went for a scan here and it was decided he would go back to Brentford, doing more testing on him,” Hallgrimsson explained.

“We will wait to see what their experts will say on it, but at least he is not in our squad for the game.”.

The Republic boss agreed Collins’ absence will be a big miss, adding: “But we have shown now that our depth is much better and the knowledge of what we are doing is much better than it has been.”.

Kosovo are in the driver’s seat, one point clear of Ireland, who are also hoping to propel themselves into pot two for the upcoming Euro 2028 draw with victory at the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday night.

They lost the reverse fixture in Pristina 1-0 but demonstrated plenty of promise in Linz, despite the result, and Hallgrimsson is eager to replicate those efforts.

“We need to get the same mentality, the same characters on the pitch against Kosovo,” he remarked.

“It is going to be as tough a game as it was in Austria, so just transfer that same attitude and if we do that we will have a good by-product, which is a win.

“It is clear we need to win the game, a draw will do nothing for us and that is our mentality going into the game.”.

Hallgrimsson has no other fresh injury concerns after James Abankwah got over a cramp concern.

The Icelandic boss was full of praise for Caoimhin Kelleher, who has been a standout throughout the campaign and made several critical stops on Saturday.

The Brentford goalkeeper is aware of the impact a win could have on qualifying for what would be a home European Championships in 2028 but insists the focus remains on the immediate future.

He stated: “Yeah, it would obviously be hard to describe, it would be an amazing experience, to play in a major tournament at home would be special.

According to recent reports, “But I don’t think we can think too far ahead into that. Obviously we’ve got to focus on tomorrow and trying to get a good result and we’ll look towards that then when it comes.

“But we all know the opportunity that’s there for us if we can perform, so it’ll be a great opportunity.”.

England's Blues brothers - how the Bellinghams helped save Birmingham

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week.

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

Sources indicate that on match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

It has been revealed that "They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them.".

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

That could all change on Thursday.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," noted Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up.

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand.

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

Yet the mood is changing at St Andrew's.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are prepares for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a fresh stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe.".

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's.

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of Â£20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least Â£10m., external.

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club.".

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun., external.

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'.

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish.".

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way.".

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid Â£3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported Â£4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022.

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley remarked: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how crucial the club is to them.".

According to recent reports, jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's.

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," mentioned Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again.".

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media, external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing.".

BBC reporter John Watson has been finding out why Bellingham is proving so popular with football fans across the world.

#995. Breaking: Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career.
  • It was just what they needed at just the right time.
  • BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career.

It was just what they needed at just the right time. For a tricky first half and beyond, Elversberg had been a stone in Borussia Dortmund’s shoe, the promoted side not just keeping the home team at bay but keeping them honest, nourishing ambitions of their own. “The fatigue was clearly visible,” the sporting director, Ole Book, noted to Sky after a week which had contained Der Klassiker in Munich and a hard-fought Champions League victory against Betis. “We were a bit too focused on managing the game, which was understandable.”.

Enter Felix Nmecha. BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference. It is a gap which has been widened by Dortmund being far from prolific, a facet which looked as if it might undercut their efforts to roll over their visitors on Saturday, especially in the absence of the injured centre-forward Serhou Guirassy.

Somebody was needed to break it open, and it was Nmecha. With two majestic sweeps of his right foot, two rockets from outside the area, he won the game for his team. His decisive moments of elevated quality pulled BVB away from their opponents when the game threatened to drift. “In terms of talent, qualities, and technique, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world,” Book beamed. “Add to that his finishing ability, and there aren’t many who are better.” That they go into the international break neck-and-neck with Bayern is all down to their No 8.

Sources indicate that after scoring, Nmecha pointed to the sky, then mimed lifting a crown from his head and placing it on the ground. It was nothing newly introduced. He did the same, also in front of the Südtribune, the yawning, world-famous 24,000-capacity terrace in which much of the club’s hardcore support stand, after scoring against Paderborn in September. It was the same celebration that Nmecha used when he struck Germany’s opening goal of the World Cup against Curaçao.

In a recent development, the celebration is a nod to Ballers in God (SIGNIFICANT), the Christian group founded “to use the global platform of football to make Jesus known”, and in particular to their campaign The King’s Return. Yet this latest display provoked a response from BVB’s fan and support department. “When it comes to the values of our club,” it remarked in a statement the day after the Elversberg game, “discrimination, and the question of what kind of societal image of humanity is given space within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.”.

The German public broadcaster ARD has linked BIG to ultra-conservative positions on issues including homosexuality and transgender identity. “Footballers are role models for millions of people, especially children and young people,” the fan and support department continued. “If this reach conveys content that excludes certain groups in society, we cannot dismiss this as merely private religious practice. Where religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, our tolerance for intolerance ends.”.

Reports suggest the club has been in dialogue with Nmecha since the Paderborn game, and a statement issued in response to Kicker’s inquiries said those talks would continue – while defending Nmecha. “For Borussia Dortmund, it is essential to take the concerns and needs of the fanbase seriously and to address them,” the club said. “Naturally, we also take the current media coverage and the associated questions and discussions very seriously.” Dortmund appear to have been careful not to use any images of the celebration on the club’s official social channels.

Recent findings suggest that these complications and this dialogue have been almost a constant since Nmecha arrived in June 2023, as a de facto Jude Bellingham replacement. His faith had already been a key part of his social media messaging and, as his transfer from Wolfsburg neared completion, some fan groups voiced their opposition, pointing to Nmecha’s sharing of anti-trans posts by the American rightwinger Matt Walsh, among others. A bright yellow banner was hung outside Signal Iduna Park sprayed with the message “@BVB Steh zu deinen worten”, a message to the club to “stick by your words”. In June 2023 Nmecha posted: “I genuinely love ALL people and don’t discriminate against anyone.”.

Dortmund’s motto, or marketing strapline, of Echte Liebe (true love), has been used in the past decade-plus to quantify exactly what makes the club special to audiences all over the world. What BVB believe elevates them is a connection with the fans, a mutual respect and understanding that goes way beyond what has increasingly become a manufacturer-customer relationship in modern times. Engaging with supporter concerns is important everywhere in German football and, arguably at Dortmund, there is a commercial imperative to visibly do so.

It was reported widely at the time of his arrival that Nmecha had a clause written into his contract that gave Dortmund the power to fine him if he made social media posts which they felt contradicted the club’s values. The club again had words with the player in 2025 after he posted a message of condolence to the family of Charlie Kirk (Nmecha deleted another post which noted Kirk had “peacefully stood up for his beliefs and values”).

Travis Kelce is taking some bench time.

Industry observers note that the Kansas City Chiefs’ tight end exited the team’s Nov. 15 match up against the Atlanta Falcons after his very first catch of the game, suffering an apparent injury to an already tender ankle.

Recent findings suggest that while Kelce received quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ 23-yard pass, the 37-year-old was tackled by the Falcons’ DeMarcco Hellams. Kelce was slow to get up from the hit but was able to limp to the sideline without assistance where his ankle was taped by the medical team. Rather than retake the field, however, Kelce made his way to the locker room for additional evaluation.

The Chiefs noted his return to the field as questionable.

Thankfully, since he was able to complete a pass before his exit from the game, Kelce has now achieved a milestone 200 consecutive games with at least one reception.

It has been revealed that not present for the injury or latest achievement, however, was Kelce’s wife Taylor Swift. Though the Grammy winner has become a staple at the Chiefs’ home games at Arrowhead Stadium, Swift often skips Kelce’s away games, including the game at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium.

Recent findings suggest that but when she does take in the on-field action live in person, Swift is often accompanied by some pals in her VIP suite. Recently, she enjoyed an enchanting reunion with pal Karlie Kloss, who joined Swift at the Chiefs’ Nov. 8 home game against the Upcoming York Jets.

The pair—who were inseparable BFFs before a rumored growing apart in the 2010s—were all smiles and even shared a hug as they watched the game, with Kloss being joined by her and her husband Jared Kushner’s 5-year-old son Levi.

But even before they watched Swift’s guy on the Chiefs, Kloss and Swift had already proved they’d shaken off any rumored bad blood. After all, Kloss and Kushner were also on the 1,000-person guest list to witness Kelce and Swift’s nuptials in July.

And like any loyal BFF, Kloss refused to fill in any blanks spaces on what exactly went down inside Madison Square Garden.

In a recent development, “Listen, I try to protect the privacy of my friends’ personal lives,” the mom of three remarked when asked about the wedding on Today. “But what I will say is that they’re an amazing couple and I’m so happy for them.”.

For a look back at how Kelce and Swift went from missed bracelet connections to being the perfect teammates, read on.

July 2023: Make the Friendship Bracelets.

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's love story began in July 2023, when the singer's Eras Tour made a stop at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Mo.

Sources indicate that as a huge Swiftie, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end caught the show with hopes of giving Taylor a friendship bracelet with his number on it. However, he failed to complete the pass due to her pre-show rituals.

August 2025: She'd Marry Him With Paper Rings.

It has been revealed that more than two years after Travis' podcast shoutout heard 'round the world, Travis and Taylor announced they are engaged. "The Life of a Showgirl was really inspired by the energy that I felt like looking into crowds and seeing you guys every single night," she told fans in the audience. "This album probably also feels very happy and confident and free because that's the way that I get to feel every single day of my life because of my fiancé, who's here tonight.".

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

In a recent development, this would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

Sources indicate that that was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

According to recent reports, this was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”.

If the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself, in what might even be argued to be his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

Industry observers note that that was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

Sources indicate that it should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

“It was a tight match – a tough one,” Thomas Tuchel, the England manager, remarked. “We didn’t take our chances when we had chances, so it stayed a tight match. It cannot be glamorous and super-exciting [all the time]. It has to be serious and determined. We wanted a final on Sunday in Spain and we have that.”.

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. For the first hour, England dominated a Croatia side who often invited six blue shirts into their back line. Tuchel said his decision to select Dan Burn in the left-sided centre-half position over the left-footed Jarrad Branthwaite was almost split – a “51 per cent decision”.

England would break through just once, when Rogers got enough of his laces on an awkward Jude Bellingham cross deflected behind him and the shot brushed Josko Gvardiol on the way in.

England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. “Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then demonstrated a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”.

“I think I maybe underappreciated how major it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“It’s just been crazy, whether it’s messages on my phone or on social media, or people calling me, and just being in the street and everyone congratulating me.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually mentioned my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”.

Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer Romelu Lukaku has retired from international football at the age of 33.

The forward made the announcement on Monday, a day after being an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1 in the Nations League.

Lukaku had been named in the Red Devils' squad for this month's Nations League fixtures, but missed last Thursday’s 2-1 win over Turkey with a hip injury and then failed to make it off the bench against Italy.

He scored 94 goals in 135 appearances for Belgium over a run that began with his debut in 2010.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United striker revealed his decision in a statement on his official Instagram page.

“Over these 16 years, I gave everything for the national team,” Lukaku remarked. “I experienced every emotion imaginable. I was lucky enough to play alongside extraordinary teammates, to whom I will always be grateful. I want to thank them all.

In a recent development, “I also want to thank all the coaches who pushed me to give my best and trusted me to help the team. It was a wonderful journey, and I cherished every moment.

“To the Belgian fans, thank you for all the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments.

“I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was incredible. I enjoyed it immensely. I am grateful. Thank you.”.

His final Belgium appearance came in a 4-1 defeat by France last month.

He leaves the international stage six goals short of a century, having struggled with a number of injuries in recent years.

The Fenerbahce attacker was still a central figure at this summer's World Cup, finding the net against Latest Zealand, Senegal and the United States.

Those goals made him Belgium's outright leading scorer at World Cups with eight, moving him past the previous record-holder, Marc Wilmots.

Across a lengthy international career, Lukaku helped Belgium finish third at the 2018 World Cup. He also reached back-to-back European Championship quarter-finals with his country in 2016 and 2021.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brazil legend plays first half for Serie C club at age 46.

‘Is this my last one? I don’t know,’ Ronaldinho claims.

Recent findings suggest that ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.

The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.

Recent findings suggest that ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.

Recent findings suggest that “It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”.

Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.

In a recent development, it is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pochettino was appointed USA manager in September 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pochettino was appointed USA manager in September 2024.

Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.

Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.

But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.

On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.

A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.

It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.

What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.

Industry observers note that by that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (Â£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.

There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.

But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.

Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.

It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.

There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.

Six PL games that defined Carrick's Man Utd tenure.

Pochettino finalising Man Utd deal after Carrick sacking.

The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games.

Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.

When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.

According to recent reports, united liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.

On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.

While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis.

The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.

Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.

Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.

United are third bottom of the Premier League and 17th in the Champions League table.

What does Mauricio Pochettino need to succeed at Manchester United?

Since Monday, talks have been ongoing with Pochettino.

On Wednesday, Berrada contacted the US Soccer Federation to confirm the existence of the release clause and their intention to activate it.

It is understood the news did not come as a surprise to those across the Atlantic.

Pochettino had been clear with his employers about the discussions with United and - most pertinently - his intention to return to the Premier League.

While United want Pochettino in situ as soon as possible, they are respectful of the fact the USA have two fixtures against Haiti to play - the second of which is on 18 November.

If Pochettino takes charge of the second game, it is understood he will be in place at United's Carrington headquarters on 19 November - four days before they face Liverpool.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gianni Infantino will face a challenge from French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo in next year's Fifa presidential election.

National association representatives on Uefa's executive committee have invited Diallo to stand and given him their unanimous backing.

Uefa stated Diallo will stand pending formal ratification by the FFF's executive committee on Tuesday. The move follows Arsene Wenger ruling himself out of a challenge to Infantino over the weekend.

Uefa pledged in August to identify a credible alternative candidate to Infantino. That pledge came after the body stated it had lost confidence in the Swiss over his strategy to seek private investment in a organization to run the commercial aspects of the World Cup and other Fifa competitions.

A Uefa statement remarked: "Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of Fifa, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community.

Recent findings suggest that “They also called for a Fifa that places the development of the game in every region of the world at the heart of its mission, upholds the highest standards of governance and works in close partnership with its member associations, confederations and football stakeholders. They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition.”.

Diallo faces a tough challenge to unseat Infantino, who will be standing for a fourth term as Fifa president.

Infantino appeared to be on the ropes in August when his private investor blueprint was rejected by three continents and a number of key allies expressing their concern at how it had been developed.

He has since rallied support, however, and is expected to receive strong backing in Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America.

Japanese FA honorary president Kozo Tashima had earlier declared his intention to stand, as has former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega.

Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has called for a change of leadership in Fifa, claiming Infantino compares unfavourably to his predecessor Sepp Blatter, who resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption.

In quotes reported by the BBC, Klopp mentioned: "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”.

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”.

Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?
