📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tenefire fans display a banner paying tribute to Jesus de Miguel.

Tenerife played their first game since the death of striker Jesus de Miguel on an emotional day at the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez stadium.

De Miguel died at the age of 30 on 3 November, a day after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a home match in Spain's Segunda Division.

Tenerife beat bottom side Ceuta 2-0 on Sunday, with tributes to De Miguel paid both before and during the game.

Lengthy standing ovations preceded and followed a minute of silence before the match.

In the ninth minute play was stopped and a round of applause took place, while a video of De Miguel was shown in the stadium, as happened at all first- and second-tier games in Spain last weekend.

Tenerife fans displayed a banner that read: "Jesus de Miguel, 9, eternally blue and white.".

Forward Nacho Gil opened the scoring for the home side in the 40th minute and celebrated by holding up De Miguel's shirt.

Gil revealed a message written under his shirt that read: "Demi, always in our hearts.".

It has been revealed that neal Viereck scored four minutes from time as Tenerife ended a run of six games without a win. They are 14th in the table.

Tenerife's game with Granada on 7 November was postponed and the club invited fans to the stadium to pay their respects to De Miguel.

Owono was given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation for the challenge which resulted in De Miguel's death.

The federation has ruled that the game between Tenerife and Andorra, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time after the incident occurred, will not be replayed and the 2-2 score will stand.

Tenerife's Enric Gallego carried a wreath of flowers on to the pitch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that since succeeding Joe Hart as England’s No. 1 in the 2017/18 season, Jordan Pickford has seen off significant challenges from Aaron Ramsdale, Nick Pope and Dean Henderson with other keepers like Jack Butland, Fraser Forster, Sam Johnstone, Tom Heaton and Jason Steele also involved in squads.

It has been revealed that he’s used to competition. But Pickford’s age, 32, and the quality of his main challenger now, 24-year-old James Trafford, means he knows he’s now in the biggest fight of his England career to remain No 1.

Recent findings suggest that this is not to call time on Pickford’s England career. It’s actually more to celebrate that England have two exceptional goalkeepers who have huge respect for each other and will push each other.

Pickford still has a role to play. It was only back in March that we were lauding Pickford for keeping a clean sheet for 923 minutes, comfortably an England record. He then conceded only eight goals in seven World Cup games - and was unbeaten in the two Florida warm-ups. Writing Pickford off is premature.

What Sunday night’s epic events in Madrid confirmed is that Trafford is Pickford’s obvious successor and the changeover may be quicker than anticipated.

According to recent reports, trafford is probably now favourite to start for England at Euro 2028. Such headlines will drive Pickford on even more. The Wearsider is very proud, very patriotic, is understandably determined to reach a century of caps (he’s six shy) and he’s always felt slightly under-appreciated.

Pickford deserves more respect. He’s played in the semi-final of two World Cups and in the final of two European Championships. Pickford helped England overcome their fear of shootouts.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sources indicate that he saved five penalties in shootouts at four different tournaments and even took one – and scored. Such service to his country cannot be dismissed lightly.

I’ve watched Pickford closely in training, hearing the impact as he throws his body around, leaping up, often slapping his gloves together in approval at a save or simple self-encouragement.

His language is very lively at times. During one session filmed by the media at Euro 2024, Pickford was heard half-laughing, half-concerned that one failed save attempt would end up all over the internet.

Recent findings suggest that pickford is far more emotional and vocal than Trafford, partly rallying his defence but also charging himself up. He needs that adrenaline charge. Get the rave on, to quote one of his sayings.

Trafford, who grew up on a farm in Cumbria, helping his dad herd sheep, is more sanguine, more controlled, and that may appeal more to Thomas Tuchel. He’s less hyper than Pickford. He also offers more of what Tuchel wants in distribution. Growing up at Manchester City, Trafford was coached to pass out from the back. Pickford introduces his booming deliveries downfield but not always accurately. Trafford is more precise, picking out his wingers well. He can be vulnerable to the quick press, though. Trafford’s still developing.

According to recent reports, but if Trafford’s time has truly come with England, he will reflect on successfully negotiating difficult times. Re-signing for Man City after a successful two seasons at Burnley should have been a re-start, embedded as No. 1, but then Gianluigi Donnarumma arrived, and Trafford was benched. Moving to Leeds United proved inspired.

Sources indicate that it’s impossible to say that Trafford came of age in Madrid as he has to deliver week after week, minimising mistakes and improving decision-making. He’s 24, playing regularly, and will mature even more into a fine goalkeeper with great shot-stopping strengths and sound distribution.

Industry observers note that trafford certainly impressed against Spain, making reflex saves from Fermin Lopez and then the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte. It is these double saves where Trafford most impresses. Late on, protecting the 3-2 lead, Trafford watched like a hawk as Lamine Yamal glided in from the right. A keeper has to make so many decisions in such short, intense passages of play, perhaps lasting only a few seconds but demanding total concentration and swift reactions, mental and physical.

Yamal could have whipped an early shot to the near-post, so Trafford had to guard that. He then stepped across as Yamal, using Anthony Gordon and Myles Lewis-Skelly to try and mask his intentions, targeted the far-post. Trafford was equal to the threat, dropping smartly to his right, pushing Yamal’s curling strike away. He remained alive to the continued threat. Marc Cucurella now had the ball.

Industry observers note that all those drills in training, the reflex save and then jumping up for the follow-up developed the muscle memory for Trafford. Cucurella’s driven return was complicated further by a slight deviation off Ben White. Trafford readjusted in a split-second and pushed the ball around the post. Trafford truly saved the day.

According to recent reports, england’s No. 1 shirt is up for grabs now. The Nations League quarter-final in March will clarify who is the owner. If Trafford keeps delivering for Leeds, the smart money is now on him to retain it. One thing can be stated for certain: England have two very good goalkeepers.

Thomas Frank has been appointed as Crystal Palace’s latest manager on a deal running until the summer of 2029, with the Danish coach now tasked with helping the south London club climb up the Premier League table.

Frank makes his return to management in England following a difficult eight-month spell leading Tottenham, having previously spent seven successful years in charge at Brentford.

Industry observers note that palace parted manufacturer with Pierre Sage last week after managing just two victories from 10 league fixtures, leaving the south London club bottom of the Premier League during the November international break. Frank will take charge for the first time away to Coventry on Saturday.

Frank stated: "It’s an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic football club. I’m really, really looking forward to it.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I’m really looking forward to meeting them.".

Paddy McCarthy has been retained as assistant manager alongside goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who was previously part of Frank's staff at Brentford, with further backroom personnel to be confirmed.

Sage originally arrived in the summer to replace Oliver Glasner following his trophy-laden tenure at Selhurst Park, but the French coach immediately faced problems.

Joining after a successful period with Lens, Sage saw key Palace defenders Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Munoz leave before the side lost three of their opening four league games.

Although Palace advanced to the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, a solitary win in the Europa League and seven defeats across 10 Premier League matches prompted chairman Steve Parish to dismiss Sage on November 12.

Frank was picked as the ideal candidate to steer Palace away from a potential relegation scrap after overseeing multiple successful survival campaigns at Brentford.

The 53-year-old took the Bees into the top flight in 2021 before helping them establish themselves in the Premier League despite having a small budget compared to rival clubs.

However, Frank’s opportunity to succeed in a different environment at Tottenham turned out to be tough despite an encouraging opening period in north London.

Amid increasing supporter frustration and a stretch of two wins in 17 league matches, Frank was sacked on February 11. He holds the worst win record of any permanent Spurs manager in Premier League history, but now seeks to succeed at Palace.

Recent findings suggest that parish noted: "I’m delighted to be able to welcome Thomas to Crystal Palace. He has a proven track record of both creating winning teams and improving players, making him the perfect fit for our club.

"I’m confident Thomas’ extensive experience in the Premier League will help us achieve our goals for the rest of the season.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

This was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

Industry observers note that this was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. So too for Ben White, the 2022 World Cup departee who scored the third and lunged with astonishing effect in the 84th minute to block a Nico Williams shot.

It has been revealed that trafford again! 👊🏻 An excellent double save from the Leeds United keeper 🙌 https://t.co/L27oQFQO1J.

This was a performance good enough to win a World Cup final, never mind Nations League Group A3 – just a shame England neglected to get to that World Cup final in the summer. The fight in question was at half-time as the players came off and White and Fabián Ruiz first tangled and others dived in.

There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

Recent findings suggest that the defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England indicated on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

In a recent development, they all had their moments. Anthony Gordon had a strong first half. Morgan Rogers was central to the two goals England scored in the 10 minutes after the break. Anderson demonstrated that he is one of the best midfielders in the world in the hour before his red card. Spain were without Rodri and in his absence his Manchester City successor was in control.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel encouraged his players to mount a ferocious press against the best first-phase passing team in the world. Brave, but it worked beautifully and for an absorbing opening 10 minutes, Spain looked all at sea. Such was the pressure, the Spain goalkeeper Unai Simón abandoned the usual build-up strategy and released his goal-kicks to the halfway line.

Even when Spain finally found their rhythm at the mid-point of the first half, England adapted. It took them a while to manage the discomfort of being denied the ball, and the familiar rapid incursions and switches of play. The counter-attacking switch from the early period pressing Spain in their own area yielded the penalty from which Kane scored the first.

Anderson snapped into Marc Cucurella and played in Kane with a straight pass punched through the Spain lines. With all his cunning, Kane knew that he could not out-sprint Pau Cubarsi, but he could sucker him into a foul which the England captain did expertly before dispatching the penalty.

Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

According to recent reports, “This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

It has been revealed that “The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”.

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

Recent findings suggest that he mentioned: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

“I noted it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”.

Asked what beating Spain can do for England’s belief, before the draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League on Friday, Tuchel stated: “You want confidence, not only through results, but confidence through performance and the result follows.

It has been revealed that “That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got. We got it through the whole campaign of the Nations League, we trusted the process and improved our game and took steps forward match by match.

It has been revealed that “We had a fantastic result and performance in Croatia followed up by a very good performance at home against Czechia. We then got our homework done against Croatia three days ago and that’s what we always wanted.

“We wanted to come back and compete on the highest level and see how far we can push our limits and how far we can push the opponent with the way we want to play and stay true to our identity. The team did excellent.”.

England survived a Spanish fightback to round off their Nations League group-stage campaign in style with a 3-2 win over the world champions in Madrid.

Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored for the visitors with James Trafford pulling off a series of saves to prevent the hosts drawing level.

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

According to recent reports, asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel remarked: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

It has been revealed that although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Industry observers note that since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

Speaking ahead of the match, Tuchel remarked: “I think we are ready to win. Now it’s key that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength. I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never. But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that.”.

Meanwhile, fresh from lifting the World Cup in the summer, Spain have a 100% winning record in this season’s Nations League. They right now boast a staggering 43-match unbeaten run in all competitions, since losing a friendly to Colombia back in March 2024. England’s task is daunting, but not impossible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham Hotspur are to move for a new striker, as their search for goals intensifies.

The Lilywhites endured a terrible start to the season under manager Robert De Zerbi and were the last team in the Premier League to pick up a win – but after encouraging signs in recent weeks, it appears that they may have turned a corner.

With Tottenham struggling to score goals, however, a new forward has been earmarked for the January transfer window.

Spurs were stated to be interested in Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi over the summer, but with the recent France international picking up a foot injury in preseason, any move to a bigger was put on hold.

De Zerbi instead brought in Omar Marmoush from Manchester City, with the Egyptian job-sharing the No.9 role with Dominic Solanke – though the pair have just two league goals between them this term.

With the North Londoners lacking a reliable hold-up man who can also offer threat in behind, attention has turned to Igor Matanovic of Freiburg.

Speaking on the Market Madness podcast, transfer expert Ben Jacobs claimed that the Croatian is an option for a loan move in January that Spurs could explore, with Bournemouth closing the door on Kroupi leaving midseason.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Cherries sold Semenyo to Manchester City in January – though the Ghanaian international only left when his release clause was triggered – and the south coast outfit are determined not to see another talent leave in the same way this campaign.

“If [Spurs] can’t find the right target, or maybe someone with a bit more experience within the Premier League, then they can reassess in the summer,” Jacobs claimed.

“What they won’t want to do is necessarily go all in and panic buy in January for someone on a long-term contract, instead of just biding their time and waiting it out.”.

Tottenham spent around £400 million in the summer building a side that finished 17th two years running, smashing their transfer record twice and recruiting seven new faces.

Every one of De Zerbi's signings over the summer – including youngsters such as Cole Ramsey and backup goalkeeper Martin Dubravka – was signed from an English side.

Matanovic is worth €30m, according to Transfermarkt. Tottenham take on Ipswich Town when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

The past year has been... a lot. Record-breaking temperatures, devastating floods and catastrophic wildfires have brought the realities of climate change into sharp focus for people around the world. At the same time, many governments and organisations have scaled back on their climate action.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re anything like me you might be feeling it’s all a bit ‘doom and gloom’. So in this series I decided to face my climate anxiety head on and set out in search of reasons for optimism.

According to recent reports, in this first episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about what the data really show and why there are still reasons to hope.

00:00 How climate change feels overwhelming.

04:27 What the data say about renewables.

11:23 Will AI stall climate progress?

21:49 How are the world’s nations doing on climate change?

Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target.

Nature: How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown.

Nature: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change.

I’m going to be honest with you. I worry a lot.

I worry about all sorts of things. Money, friends, family, if my voice is weird as you’re listening to it... but there’s one thing I’ve been worried about since I was a teenager in the early 2000s. The climate.

Recent findings suggest that those anxieties have only gotten worse. In recent years, it has felt like climate action has stalled. In 2024, the world passed the 1.5˚C ‘threshold’ set in Paris for the first time. Shortly thereafter, Donald Trump returned to the White House and on the first day of his Presidency set about reversing climate policies of the previous administration, vowing to promote fossil fuels. In Europe, right-wing politicians have taken aim at climate goals, with the EU weakening previously ambitious environmental policy. All while it’s getting hotter and hotter. In May there were record breaking temperatures in my home of the UK , then in June those records were broken again, twice in the same week in fact, with temperatures in some places across the continent more than ten degrees hotter than they were between 1991-2020. That was the story all over Europe. Without climate change, it’s extremely unlikely Europeans would have had to endure these heatwaves. And globally, scientists of all stripes have expressed doubts that any government has done enough to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

So, it feels like we’re failing on climate, heck, I can even look outside my window and see evidence for that. But what’s weird is that even as climate change is affecting me more, I find it harder to engage with.

Recent findings suggest that as things get worse, I’m having trouble staying optimistic that we, you me and everyone, can do anything about it. And that’s an odd position to be in, as a science journalist. Climate change is one of the biggest stories of our time.

Every week, we pick out stories to cover on the podcast. And I always want to report the latest climate science, and I do, but I find it hard. Sometimes it just feels like more bad news at a time when our audience, and I, could do with less. I feel hopeless.

But is that actually right? Am I justified in that feeling? As the one thing I know about science is often the truth is a bit more complicated than we think. So, while the narrative can feel overwhelming negative, is that really what the data says?

To try and shake myself out of this climate funk, talking to some of the scientists and campaigners on the front lines of climate research, and what I found was a story of: Tipping points….

That has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge.

I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions.

The system is changing at exponential speed.

It has been revealed that this is Cooked? a three-part miniseries for Nature, where I try and find out whether we are well… cooked. Is it game over for climate or are there reasons for hope? I’m your host Nick Petrić Howe. And in this first episode, I decided to start with the data, and I had a good idea of who might be able to help me with that.

As a data scientist, I'm biased. And I would say, look at the data to understand for these big problems, where they're coming from, why they're happening, and importantly, what we can do to solve them.

Sources indicate that in the past year or so, I’ve found myself struggling with anxiety about the climate. But a couple of years ago a book came out that seemed to fly against what I had assumed was the case, as it stated, backed up with oodles of data, that it isn’t the end of the world. So, I knew I wanted to speak to its author — Hannah Ritchie.

What I wanted to do in that book was, think, twofold.

That’s Hannah, the author of ‘Not the end of the world’ and a data scientist at our World in Data and the University of Oxford.

One was that I was trying to write it to my former self, who was very, very pessimistic, wasn't sure if there was really a future there for me and present where we are now. And the point is not that these problems are solved in any way, they're still huge problems, but we have started to make progress and there's lots of opportunity for us to make more progress. My point is not that we should be complacent and optimistic that these problems will solve themselves. I think it's to kind of maybe get rid of a bit of the cynicism that there's nothing that we can do and actually no one is doing anything because I don't think that's true. And I think the second kind of motivation for doing that is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and substantial things that we need to do to solve them?

The book looked at seven huge challenges that humanity faces, including climate change, examining each through the lens of data, to understand the progress we have and haven’t made on them, and what we should do. So I was curious to hear from Hannah about how we were actually doing on climate change.

It has been revealed that if you go back 10 years, the world we were sitting in when the world signed the Paris Agreement was that the alternatives to fossil fuels were much more expensive than fossil fuels. For solar and wind were way more expensive. Batteries were extremely expensive. Electric vehicles were basically not on the radar at that point. So it seemed very, very hard to me at the time to see how the world would actually progress on this. What we've seen over the last decade is this huge drop in the costs of these low-carbon energy sources. And that now means that they're cost competitive with fossil fuels, right? So you have the kind of short-term incentive of picking the low-cost solution, now adding up and aligning with the long-term problem we're trying to solve, which is climate change.

According to recent reports, these days renewable energy is very cheap. Let’s take solar energy as an example. Between 2009 and 2025, estimates from the investment firm Lazard suggest solar energy prices have dropped to less than a sixth of what it used to cost on average. This number even includes the continued costs of running solar plants, making them, along with wind, the cheapest form of energy.

Sources indicate that this change has helped Hannah go from pessimistic to optimistic about the future of climate change. It’s not just that the costs have tumbled, more and more this ‘clean’ energy is actually being implemented as well.

We now also see that many countries are now rolling out clean energy at an increasingly fast pace. So it's not like it's just that the cost has dropped. You can actually now start to see that translating into action.

Hannah also thinks that this electrification of the world has other benefits too.

What's really key about that electrification lever, and I think is under appreciated, is how much you gain there in terms of efficiency. You know, it's not just we want to do this because it saves us carbon emissions, which it will if we were powering that through low carbon power, but also you get huge efficiency gains from this. like driving in an electric car uses about a third of the energy of driving in a petrol car, right? So you actually also get rid of lots of this energy waste that we currently have in the system.

In a recent development, worldwide, adoption rates of electric vehicles are increasing. Around a quarter of every fresh vehicle sold is electric, and in some countries this rate is much higher. In Norway 97% of new cars sold were electric, while in China 53% were. Now, many people are critical of electrical vehicles for various reasons. Mining of lithium for use in batteries can be very environmentally damaging, for instance. And using public transport is better than having a personal electric vehicle most of the time. But when it comes to their climate credentials, electric cars beat conventional every time.

Sources indicate that the world has also been built in many places to favour vehicles and in some areas public transport is not a viable option. So if we want the most people to use the least climate emission causing form of transport, electric vehicles will be part of the mix.

But it’s not just data on clean energy and electrification that gives Hannah hope. She also points to progress that’s been made in making steel and concrete production more climate conscious. They’re maybe a bit less obvious in our day to day lives, as most of us don’t work on big construction projects, but these core components of buildings come with big emissions. Cement production, for example, accounted for around 6% of global carbon emissions as of 2024 according to the International Energy Agency.

But this is down from a peak in 2021, due to slowed growth in construction, and is projected to decrease further as improvements are made to the recipe for cement, or alternatives to it entirely are created.

Industry observers note that these solutions haven't been scaled yet. They're at a very, very small level, but I think we still have made progress there and there are actually solutions starting to come online and starting to get cost competitive, but it will take some time for them to build up to a kind of level where you would actually start to see dents in the data.

Sources indicate that as Hannah remarked, the point of her book and this examination of the data is not to allow us all to pat ourselves on the back and say ‘job’s a good ‘un’. There’s still a lot that we need to do, and in many ways some of these changes aren’t happening fast enough. Rather the point is to not make us feel despondent and hopeless, as that helps nobody.

And there are actually reasons for optimism. Falling prices in renewables, increased electrification and more climate-conscious construction are all starting to make dents in the data according to Hannah.

So maybe I don't need to be so worried after all. assuming of course that we can keep this up.

Renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is making the rise in emissions less bad.

There's a fresh disruptive and energy-intensive technology out there that could stall climate progress. Artificial intelligence.

It has been revealed that the level of debate about this technology is massive. It's actually really fascinating because I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

According to recent reports, whenever I open social media these days, I see a lot of scepticism about artificial intelligence. I don’t have to scroll far to come across a video of someone pretending to be a large language model powered chatbot who says silly things while chugging litres of water. But the backlash against the technology is spilling out of social media and pouring into real world legislation. We've seen the first moratoriums on the building of data centres, the facilities that house the infrastructure for AI and other internet services. And often the cited reasons are environmental — water and electricity use.

So that got me wondering, if AI is so energy intensive could it stall climate progress? Especially as many of these data centres are using fossil fuels to meet their energy needs. For the sake of this podcast, I’m just going to focus on energy demands, as that’s what’s more relevant to the climate, and put other environmental concerns to one side for now.

According to recent reports, to do so, I wanted to put those memes aside as well and find out what the data actually says. So, I reached out to an expert on data centres and their energy use to go through some of the numbers.

My name is Ketan Joshi. I'm an independent researcher and analyst, working on energy and data centres and fossil fuel phase-out.

Ketan has been working as energy analyst for many years, but more recently has been focusing on how much energy data centres consume, particularly for artificial intelligence. I wanted to know how a growth in data centres would affect the climate, but he explained to me that that’s a quite a difficult thing to work out.

Sources indicate that we have thousands of projections of data center growth into the near future. But the level of variation that you see in these projections makes me almost want to never use them. and the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway, you know, it'll grow to maybe four to five percent by twenty thirty. I've seen ones that are up to like twenty percent of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway. You know, it'll grow to maybe 4 to 5% by 2030. I've seen ones that are up to like 20% of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind this wild skew of future projections is because there is an inherent assumption about the future of artificial intelligence and the shape and form that it takes in the near future. The way that we tend to formulate projections just falls apart with something like this where there is an inherent uncertainty as to what the technology is, what it's going to be used for, whether it's hype, whether it's real, whether we go for high energy consumption models or low energy consumption models. There's like 10 crisscrossing vectors of uncertainty that make it really, really hard to say what's going to happen.

The future is, unfortunately, unpredictable. It’s hard to know what AI will look like in 10 years, or even 10 days for that matter. So, it’s tough to fit into our projections of the future and how it may impact the climate. As a result, Ketan likes to focus on the here and now to see what we can understand about the technology. To start, it’s important to note that while AI gets a lot of attention, it presently forms a small part of energy usage. The International Energy Agency, for instance, estimates that data centres use — for everything, not just AI — around 2% of the world’s energy. As Ketan claims, that may grow — perhaps by a lot, perhaps by not so much. It’s part of the uncertainty with the technology.

According to Ketan’s analyses, though, AI and by that, I mean the generative kind that powers chatbots, may be particularly energy intensive.

Something that I've found in the past few weeks actually, having looked at some of the new newer corporate statements. So for instance, Microsoft analyzed their latest statement, I analyzed Google and Amazon. And all three of those companies are using more energy to earn the same amount of revenue, if that makes sense.

Rather than working towards more efficiency as computing has done in the past, Ketan thinks that companies are using more and more energy to try and make cleverer chatbots, or autonomous AI agents. Google and Microsoft for example, have acknowledged that they’ve increased their energy usage as they build out AI capacity.

One thing to note here is that different use cases of AI have different energy demands. Techniques like Machine Learning which often gets labelled AI, don't use as much energy as generative AI like Large Language Models. And then within generative AI, things like a written response from a chatbot needs a lot less energy than generating an image or a video.

But the concern for the climate is that all this energy needs to come from somewhere. And if there isn’t sufficient renewable energy in place, it will come from fossil fuels.

Sources indicate that figuring out how much data centres may be using fossil fuels, though, is not easy. Ketan explained to me that when companies report their power consumption it’s not quite as simple as them just stating what proportion of renewable energy versus fossil fuels they’ve used. Similarly to carbon offsets, companies can purchase certificates from renewable energy providers and then use them to show that their emissions are lower than they are. Microsoft recently stopped using this method, which has been widely criticised, and in their most recent report there was a large rise in their emissions.

It has been revealed that the companies can also have positive effects on renewable energy. With their vast resources they can fund fresh wind and solar farms. Microsoft, for example, has announced a $6 billion agreement to build AI infrastructure powered by renewables in Norway. Deals such as these can also then be included in companies’ reports on what kinds of energy they use.

So, untangling all of this is pretty tricky. With that in mind, Ketan explained how energy use has changed in the US, where there’s the most data centres in the world.

There's a newly introduced report from the energy information administration, updating on 2025 data. And of course, you know, emissions have gone up. They haven't gone up crazy. Like they haven't gone, you know, it's not like it’s skyrocketing, you know, right angle, but they have gone up and renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is just making the rise in emissions less bad.

The report Ketan mentioned says that US energy-related CO2 emissions went up by about 2% in 2025. That may not sound like a lot, but it’s against a backdrop of emissions falling, so any rise is a cause for concern for the climate. And like Ketan says, renewable energy adoption has continued apace, so the fact that there were more renewables, but emissions still went up implies that more energy was coming from carbon-emitting fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that this is backed up by a report from the Energy Institute, a UK-based professional body that monitors energy use. The report noted that US emissions had increased in 2025 due to higher coal use, and that electricity demand had risen faster than supply driven in part by data centres and artificial intelligence. An independent research firm, the Rhodium group, also identified a rise in carbon emissions in the US and cited a particularly cool winter, more coal use and increased demand in electricity from data centres as reasons.

Of course, data centres could be powered by renewable energy, but building this supply takes time and if we have a sudden increase in energy demand, due to AI for instance, then fossil fuels could be used to plug the gap. Google, for example, has acknowledged that it’s expanding its AI development on a grid that is undersupplied with clean energy, but still remains a large funder of clean energy projects. Google still intends to reduce their emissions, but right now, they’re using more fossil fuel energy.

Ketan would like to see more transparency from the tech companies creating AI on its environmental impacts, so it can be scrutinised more easily, along with more regulation from governments. He also thinks that everyone has a role to play deciding on what terms we use this technology.

In a recent development, ketan is actually optimistic about the future, as it seems that the general public are beginning to understand that they do have the power to demand better from these companies. Environmental, cost and climate concerns are being raised against AI, and politicians are listening — you can look to the growth of moratoriums on data centres to see that. To be clear this isn’t just because of climate, opponents of data centres describe them as being ugly, straining local resources and not providing many tangible benefits to their residents. These are issues that affect people no matter what side of the political divide they sit on. And this bipartisan opposition has meant that politicians have started taking action.

But that touches on another thing I wondered about. What are governments and nations actually doing? Are they meeting the goals they’ve set out for climate? And it’s certainly felt to me like there’s been some backsliding recently — with right-wing politicians taking aim at climate goals.

So, what does the data say about how the nations of the world are doing?

Well, it's better than we used to think 10 years ago, but it's definitely not there where it should be.

If you’ve ever engaged with climate change, you’ll know that it’s a global issue. The whole world is getting hotter and that affects all of us. Because of that, nations often get together and come up with various pledges on what they’re going to do about that. What comes out of these pledges is ultimately what we, as a global society, are doing about climate change.

And I knew a scientist who keeps close tabs on this, so I gave him a call.

It has been revealed that hello. Niklas Höhne, Latest Climate Institute, calling in from Cologne, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that I met Niklas a few years ago at COP26, the enormous climate conference run by the UN. He co-founded the Latest Climate Institute, a non-profit that works on climate policy, where he oversees analyses on climate policy. I was there reporting for Nature and I asked him, even back then, if things were hopeless. I remember that he didn’t coddle me or make me despair. He gave a nuanced picture. So, I caught up with him to see where we are now.

Recent findings suggest that so while 10 years ago we thought global greenhouse gas emissions would rise forever and would lead to a temperature increase of three and half degrees by the end of the century, we now think that with currently implemented policies, they will stabilize and decline and then lead to around two and a half degrees by the end of the century. So a full degree better than we thought only 10 years ago. So that's remarkable. That's really good. But it's not enough. The Paris agreement says well below two or in the direction of 1.5 and there we are far away from it. And also, we have to say that in the past years, global greenhouse gas emissions have still increased. So despite all of the efforts, is still more fossil fuels being burned each year and therefore we have more greenhouse gas emissions each year and that means not only are we not stopping climate change, we are fuelling climate change. So, we are accelerating the speed of change each year by adding more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere than we had in the year before.

The main driver of this drop in the projected temperature increase.

is something that Hannah already touched on — the speed of renewable energy production.

Prices are falling and Niklas thinks this may push us to precipice to start some exponential change.

Sources indicate that niklas Höhne: I think the last 10 years we've been surprised each year about the speed of renewable energy, electrification and the transformation that has been started. So, I assume that also next year and the years after we will be positively surprised because the end of that development of the technologies is not there. Yeah. So, prices still decline. Upcoming battery technologies are invented. Renewables are incredibly cheap compared to 10 years and are still declining. And what we as humans often underestimate is exponential change. The system is changing at exponential speed. And that means each year more solar is implemented than we thought before or more batteries are implemented, more electric cars. And most of the models, they are still kind of assuming a linear change and underestimate the speed of the transformation. And that's why I think I'm quite optimistic about our future projections that this renewable energy transformation will actually win against the fossil fuels because it's simply exponential change. And that always has to win over a linear trend, which is the one described by the fossil fuels.

You can see a similar exponential change if you look at the history of cars.

It has been revealed that at the turn of the twentieth century there was blight on cities — horses. According to the London Transport museum in 1900 there were 300,000 horses in London. But just 14 years later they’d all but disappeared. This sudden departure of the city’s workhorses helped humanity solve a pretty relevant problem for a climate podcast — pollution.

Horses produced a lot of… waste — you know the kind of waste I'm talking about — that was very literally clogging up streets. The solution, ironically, given the topic of the podcast, was cars. Motorized vehicles had actually been around for a few years in the early 20th Century, but it wasn’t really until 1908 when the Model-T ford came out, the first car affordable to a large number of people, that they really took off. In 1910 there were 8000 cars registered in London, in 1920 there were 190,000, the next year there were 250 000 And as cars took off, streets once clogged with horse manure instead became roads for motorcars.

That may seem like a pretty inevitable change, but if you were a Londoner in 1900, you’d probably wouldn’t have believed that the world could be so different in a few decades.

Perhaps renewable energy will be the same for us. It may seem like we’ll never overcome our addiction to fossil fuels, but as prices tumble, maybe we’re standing on the cliff edge of that exponential change.

So there are certainly positives for the climate. The speed of the energy transition has taken many experts by surprise. But beyond that, there’s still a long to go. And when it comes to how countries are actually sticking to their climate pledges, it was a bit of a mixed bag.

We regularly look at who is basically the best, which is the best country around the world. And the places one, two, three are always empty. So, no country is doing everything correct. But in each area, you can see quite positive things. We have electric mobility, which is shooting off and was shooting off in Norway because Norway supported it significantly with a lot of money. But now it's basically the better way of doing things. So even countries like Vietnam or Nepal have very high adoption rates for electric cars. They sell more electric cars than conventional vehicles in these countries. And that is remarkable because it reveals that this is the most economic way of having individual mobility. Then there's other areas, buildings and industry, which really are a bit behind. And it's very difficult to find really good examples where countries are really doing well. But OK, I think also in buildings and in industry, this idea of electrification is something that will now take off as well. So in buildings, it's heat pumps for heating, which are the new normal. So, there's huge opportunity to do more in those areas as well.

Recent findings suggest that you may have noticed that some of the biggest emitters haven’t been mentioned there. And to be honest, they were some of the ones I was most worried about. China and the US.

China is the world’s top emitter according to the International Energy Agency, but it seems that their emissions are finally starting to peak — meaning that the greenhouse gases they emit may be starting to reduce. According to some analyses, they have already peaked. This is likely because they have implemented a huge amount of renewable energy. Last year, China installed more solar capacity than the rest of the world combined, although this boom in installation is slowing down a bit now.

In a recent development, and as Niklas explained to me, China has also been instrumental in producing what the world needs for renewable energy — they’re the leading manufacturer of solar, wind and battery technology. But he did impress on me that that wouldn’t have been possible without the policies of several countries, especially in Europe, promoting renewables and therefore creating the right market conditions for China.

And then there’s world’s second biggest emitter and the largest historical contributor to climate change. The US. There I was worried about the influence of the most recent administration. Trump’s Team has dealt a severe blow to the world’s ability to tackle climate change, by walking away from Paris Agreement on Climate, for the second time. They also repealed the ‘endangerment finding’ that set out that climate change is a public threat and has been used to enact climate policy. And they have spent billions trying to undo climate projects, giving the companies behind them refunds if they instead invest that money in fossil fuels. These actions, the administration say, would save the United States money by removing excess regulations, lower bills for families and help maintain the US’s leadership. But they are counter to what climate scientists say we should be doing — we need to stop burning fossil fuels and rein in our emissions.

So, I was expecting a pretty negative response from Niklas when I asked about how the US is doing. But he had a few surprises for me.

So for the US as such, it's the second largest emitter and the Trump administration has basically dismantled all climate policies that were there from the federal government in the US. And that means now that the emissions in the US will still continue to decline, but will decline slower.

This first surprise, is that while the actions of the Trump administration will likely increase the emissions that the US will produce, that is against a backdrop of overall decline. Even though there's been a recent uptick in emissions in the past year, the US's emissions have been steadily falling since the early 2000s and that will likely continue. Albeit not as fast as it would if the Trump administration was more pro climate. Ultimately, the economics of clean energy are hard even for the most powerful country in the world to fight against — it’s getting harder and harder to justify the use of fossil fuels when the alternatives are cheaper.

The second surprise was an unexpected way that the current US administration may have unintentionally pushed for a move away from fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that which is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. And that created a significant energy crisis with very, very high fossil fuel prices for oil and gas. And that created a push towards energy efficiency and renewable energy. And that effect will be significant. It's very difficult to quantify that right now. But from our point of view, it's very clearly that that will has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge, so to say, and over the tipping point that it will be self-propelling because all the countries that currently suffer significantly from fuel shortage is not even a price, a high price is really a shortage that simply have not enough. They will now really, really think about alternatives and have already. So, some countries have already increased their renewable energy targets. China has reduced their oil consumption by 10 to 20%, depending on which source you look at within only 12 months. So, there's significant changes on the way that will reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

According to recent reports, as Niklas mentioned, data on this is hard to get, and this is still an evolving story. Time will tell what the impacts of the war in Iran may be. There have in fact been moves towards and away from renewable energy as a result of surging oil and gas prices — with nations like India and South Korea burning more coal in response to the higher gas prices, while people in the Philippines have taken to installing rooftop solar panels at record rates to avoid the high oil prices. So, a true accounting of the effect of the closure of the strait of Hormuz will take some time. But Niklas’s assessment is backed up by an increased sale of electric vehicles and a record high in solar exports from China, and an analysis by Carbon Brief that suggests that global emissions may fall in 2026. This has led some to wonder whether the war in Iran will be a tipping point for energy — that it will finally end humanity’s addiction to fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that overall, while there are clearly some areas in which the world is behind on its targets, it’s perhaps not as dire as I thought. In terms of renewable energy, adoption is accelerating. True, the current pace won’t be enough to meet our climate goals. We need to stop emitting carbon altogether, and soon if we're to meet the 1.5° target set in Paris, and even then we'll probably have to take some carbon out of the atmosphere. But Niklas, even with all the caveats, was optimistic about the future.

We have all the tools at hand and even now it's economic and the obstacle is not technology, the obstacle is not cost. The obstacle is our inertia in the system and that some lose something and some others gain something. And that is something we as a society really have to overcome.

In a recent development, so, while there’s still a long way to go, there are reasons for optimism. Renewable energy has outperformed many researchers expectations, and continues to do so, in spite of the backlash against it in some quarters. Which, I’ll be honest, does make me feel better. The data tell me that it’s not completely hopeless. When cities were overwhelmed by horses and their waste, cheap motor vehicles changed things in a matter of decades. I’m hopeful that renewable energy can do the same here.

But this is what the data notes, largely about what we’ve already done. I was also curious about what we should do in the future. What are some of the substantial ideas that can help tackle climate change? That’s next time.

According to recent reports, we could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. But I think having very good affordable substitutes for people to switch to is just really, really crucial.”.

#927. Tech Report: The moment that galvanised England to deliver major statement against Spain

Tech Report: The moment that galvanised England to deliver major statement against Spain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Spain vs England was a game that had almost everything, and may yet mean more; perhaps the most significant moment might have come before it had even started.
  • The hosts took the opportunity of a first match back in Madrid since the World Cup to showcase the trophy, in what almost felt another homecoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Spain vs England was a game that had almost everything, and may yet mean more; perhaps the most significant moment might have come before it had even started.

The hosts took the opportunity of a first match back in Madrid since the World Cup to showcase the trophy, in what almost felt another homecoming.

The mood was very much of revelling in their embossed status, something that would have had a particular edge for this specific nation.

No country that has won the World Cup has waited as long for another trophy as England.

And, as the 2010 winners Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente presented Unai Simon that with that precious piece of brilliant gold, it was almost literally in England’s faces.

Thomas Tuchel’s side had to watch the goalkeeper wave the World Cup about right in front of them.

Industry observers note that it had been noted on the Spanish side that Jude Bellingham was the only player who clapped, this now being the city that he calls home with Real Madrid. He then played like he was demanding the same appreciation, and he was not the only one.

As one figure with knowledge of the England camp said: “They will have been thinking ‘that’s what we want’.”.

Seeing the World Cup so close and yet so far, with more than three years until the next edition, only deepened a mood that had been felt in the build-up to this game.

England, in the words of both Declan Rice and Thomas Tuchel, knew they were going to win.

“I could feel the true belief in the dressing room before the match that this is exactly the moment where we want to prove ourselves and push our limits,” the manager remarked.

They had that conviction to show what they were really about, and to show they would be the only team in the world not cowed by Spain. It was that mentality that comes when you feel ready to beat a rival that has long had it over you; that has been a benchmark.

A pace was set just moments after seeing that trophy, as a ferocious England subjected Simon to a flurry.

Just as importantly, they displayed a upcoming level of their own, even beyond Tuchel describing it as the best performance of his time.

This wasn’t, after all, the usual counter-attacking approach to playing Spain - at least not for when England actually got so far ahead.

It was England imposing their game, an evolving ideology, on Spain.

“We are well aware which steps we took after the World Cup,” Tuchel said, conspicuously repeating this more than once.

The manager was deeply stung after all the criticism following the Argentina defeat.

And yet, much as he might bristle about it in public, it does feel as if some of that criticism has been acknowledged.

England look much more technical, but still with pace.

Throughout the World Cup, after all, there was a definite sense of his team just seeking to force their way through.

This was something much more considered and coherent.

“We wanted to get better in the deep build-up, we wanted to get better at defending in a low block and on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play on every opponent,” Tuchel remarked.

This similarly feeds into another theme of the night, which was how James Trafford’s performance may start a path that sees him become England’s No 1.

It was conspicuous that, when asked about the goalkeeper’s brilliant late double-save, Tuchel immediately pointed to his pure football effect.

“But there was a lot to do in the deep build-up as well, to overcome the first line of press, which he did very well with everyone around him,” he noted. “So there was a lot to do, never lose the concentration, never lose the focus, never lose the vision, to find the free man to overcome the press and put the game into the opponent’s half.”.

Tuchel clearly wants to change the very focus of this team.

And, in doing so, he wants to change its entire outlook.

There was naturally a lot of talk about “confidence” after a victory like this, which Tuchel was only too happy to immerse himself in.

Industry observers note that “You want confidence, not only through results but confidence through performance and the result follows,” Tuchel stated. “That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got.”.

That’s also what goes much deeper.

When Spain beat France in the World Cup semi-final with what was the performance of the tournament - “the statement performance” as Tuchel would have it - some close to Didier Deschamps’s squad felt the reason for the win had actually come much earlier.

Spain had beaten France in a series of high-profile games, above all the Euro 2024 and World Cup 2026 semi-finals. Lamine Yamal had been right to emphasise that, because he knew it played on French minds.

Sources indicate that it gave Spain an edge. They knew they could beat France, but France were unsure if they could beat Spain.

That’s also why the frantic ending to this game in Madrid, so at odds with the first hour, may have been so important.

Had Spain equalised, or potentially won, England would have just been another team to fail to beat them. It could similarly have been the deepening of England’s own complex about Spain, since this would have been three high-profile set-backs in succession.

Even if this had just been a draw, after all, it would have felt like a defeat given it was a 3-0 lead.

It was a win, and a first defeat that Spain have endured in 44 games over two and a half years.

As such, England are not just another team the Spanish are reigning over.

They’re a team that know how to beat them, that can carry that through to a home Euros.

It might even create a bit of consideration on the Spanish side, even allowing for how assured they are in their own approach.

It might be the beginning of a proper modern rivalry.

Might, of course. England have to go and use this to do what Spain have made customary, and actually win one of those trophies.
