#925. Breaking: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 27m • 📚 Deep Dive (5434 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that who is football’s most legendary No 9?
  • Sources indicate that the relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them.
  • One is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it.

Sources indicate that the relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

One is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire. Nobody stood out quite like Yashin, the almost mythical USSR and Dinamo Moscow goalkeeper of the 1950s and 1960s. He often wore a flat cap in goal, and his trademark kit led to the nicknames “Black Spider” or “Black Panther” (strictly speaking, it should have been the less catchy Very Very Dark Blue Spider). Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the Ballon d’Or; with a respectful nod to Dino Zoff, Peter Schmeichel and others, he was a simple choice.

Industry observers note that it would be a crime against dynamism and flair if we didn’t give one of the traditional full-back numbers to a Brazilian. Some of their great right-backs didn’t actually wear No 2 – Djalma Santos and Carlos Alberto, World Cup-winners of 1958 and 1970, sported No 4 – but that still leaves us with the richest pickings. It’s hard to look beyond Cafu, a bullet train on the right for Brazil, Roma, Milan and others. He won two World Cups and is the only man to play in three consecutive finals. Chuck in more than 700 club games, and that’s a mind-boggling amount of runs up that right flank.

Few could dispute this choice. Maldini is No 3. Milan retired his number – it can only be used again if one of his sons plays for the club – and it’s almost a surprise Fifa didn’t do the same. As a left-back or left-sided centre-back, Maldini came as close as anyone to perfecting defending; on the ultra-rare occasions he was given a chasing, by Chris Waddle or Karel Poborsky, it was a JFK moment. It’s an oddity that he didn’t wear No 3 at Italia 90 or USA 94. But for most of his career, to see Maldini with any other number would have been like seeing James Bond in a shell suit.

For longevity and sheer class – on and off the field – Zanetti pips Pep Guardiola, Sergio Ramos and the aforementioned Brazilian right-backs to this number. A Swiss Army knife of a footballer, Zanetti was one of the first players to show that the positions of right-back and centre-midfield spoke the same language. He won 16 trophies in 19 years at Inter, 15 of them as a quietly inspirational captain. José Mourinho mentioned “it was an honour to coach him”, while Maldini called him “my most respected enemy”. As was the case with Maldini, Zanetti’s number was retired by a Milanese giant.

Recent findings suggest that with apologies to Zinedine Zidane, Fabio Cannavaro and Obdulio Varela, the terrifying and granite-willed captain of Uruguay’s 1950 World Cup winners, this was never in doubt. Beckenbauer, libero and captain of the all-conquering West Germany and Bayern Munich sides of the 1970s, was born to stroll around a football field, No 5 on his back, an imaginary Andrex-soft sax jazz soundtrack playing in the background. His biographer, Uli Hesse, wrote that the number “became synonymous with his unique interpretation of the libero role”. Nobody did it better; nobody ever will, which is essentially why, quite rightly, Bayern retired their No 5 shirt in December 2024.

According to recent reports, iconography trumps tactics on this one. In modern football, a No 6 is a deep-lying midfielder, but in the 20th century it was indelibly associated with a specific genre of centre-back: captains, leaders, legends. The list is headed by Bobby Moore, Tony Adams and the don; Baresi, a manager on the field for Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello during Milan’s golden age, his shirt retired by the club in 1997. Baresi died this year; if you have any doubts that he is the definitive No 6, just look at the pictures from his funeral in August of this year.

This probably should have been given to Garrincha, who wore No 7 when he single-footedly won the 1962 World Cup for Brazil, but you can’t argue with a trademark. Never mind the trifling matter of almost 1,000 career goals, CR7 is a brand that includes fragrances, underwear, footwear, lifestyle hotels, a fitness app … even bottled water. It all started in 2003, when Sir Alex Ferguson encouraged the teenager from Portugal to embrace one of the most iconic shirts in football – Manchester United No 7s include George Best, Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and David Beckham. On a global scale, Ronaldo, now retired from international duty, is the most famous of the lot.

Industry observers note that desailly embraced the No 8 shirt when he was repurposed as a central midfielder at Milan then wore it when he played centre-half for the France team that won France 98 and Euro 2000. Desailly won the lot as a No 8, with the enduring memory of him in that number coming from the 1994 Champions League final, as the then 25-year-old rampaged through Barcelona to score the final goal. Xavi, for Spain, Andrés Iniesta, for Barcelona, and Socrates were strong shouts, all more traditional No 8s, but Desailly got the nod.

Industry observers note that A choice that was painfully obvious, romantic and a bit dispiriting. Let’s start with the good stuff: Ronaldo 1.0 was the greatest young player we’ve ever seen, blessed like nobody before or since with the holy trinity of power, speed and skill. The dispiriting bit is that his Nike Mercurial R9 boots, unveiled in the buildup to France 98, catalysed an age of naked commercialism that football has never escaped. (Paradoxically, Ronaldo was wearing No 10 for Inter at the time, though that would soon change.) Let’s just remember the good stuff – R9, the first PlayStation footballer, and the platonic ideal of a distinctly Brazilian brilliance.

“No matter what happens and no matter who is in charge, the No 10 shirt will always be mine.” We’re not going to argue with Maradona, even if Lionel Messi, Pelé or Ferenc Puskas were the most compelling alternatives. To Maradona, the No 10 was a way of life, part of a uniquely Argentinian identity – that of the pibe, the creative genius from a poor background blessed with celestial skill and the vicious defiance of an alley cat. He even had the No 10 tattooed on his back. Close your eyes and you can probably see the font.

“I remember the first time I saw him,” said Sir Alex Ferguson. “He was 13 and just floated over the ground like a cocker spaniel chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind.” Giggs wore a lot of different numbers at the start of his career – 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 – but from the moment the Premier League introduced squad numbers in 1993, he was Manchester United’s No 11, even when he changed position in his dotage. There were other 24-carat contenders, including the Brazilian collective of Garrincha, Rivellino, Eder, Romario, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho, but none can match Giggs’s longevity or medal collection.

In a recent development, after an injury-ruined season with Milan, Van Basten started Euro 88 on the bench, both literally and numerically. He came in for the second game against England, scored a hat-trick and never looked back. A Hitchcockian late winner against the hosts, West Germany, was followed by an entirely preposterous volley in the final against USSR. From then on he was the Netherlands’ No 9. But the legend of No 12 endured, particularly when Thierry Henry was playing for France: he chose No 12 because of Van Basten. Were it not for the Dutchman, another Frenchman, the great Alain Giresse, would have been our choice.

The German sense of humour has always been underrated: they, more than any other country, have embraced the No 13 shirt. It’s been worn at major tournaments by Rudi Völler, Karl-Heinz Riedle, Michael Ballack, Thomas Müller – and Gerd Müller. He picked it for the 1970 and 1974 World Cups, and a triumphant Euro 72, as a nod to his childhood hero, Max Morlock, who scored in the 1954 World Cup final win over Hungary. Muller played 13 World Cup games and almost finished with 13 goals. The alternative ending was better: his 14th, in the 1974 final against the Netherlands, won the World Cup.

Cruyff’s first encounter with No 14 came by chance. Ajax’s Gerrie Muhren couldn’t find his usual No 7 shirt, so Cruyff gave him the No 9 and pulled the first spare shirt out of the bag. Ajax won, Cruyff kept wearing No 14 and embraced every connection: for example, he’d married his wife, Danny, on 2 December 1968 and pointed out that 2+12 and 6+8 both equal 14. The Cruyff Foundation later set up Schoolyard14, the key principle of which is the 14 Rules of Johan Cruyff. If he were a young footballer in 2026, Cruyff would be the first to have a symbol instead of a number.

This was the toughest of the teens, with nobody demanding selection. We plumped for a man who, as far as we can tell, spent only five games in the No 15 shirt. Falcão, an imperious box-to-box playmaker, missed all Brazil’s World Cup qualifiers for Spain 82 – Roma didn’t have to release him, so they didn’t – and as a result was not among Nos 1-11. But he played all five games at the tournament in the No 15 shirt and won the Silver Ball, which makes him officially the best player in the greatest attacking team many of us have ever seen.

According to recent reports, sham! Yes, it’s somewhat awkward having a certain era of Manchester City players on this list given “events” a few weeks ago, but, equally, it’s impossible to ignore them entirely given their achievements on the pitch, and that’s very much the case when it comes to Rodri, a man who completed football by the age of 30. He’s won the World Cup, the Euros, the Ballon d’Or, the Golden Ball, the Treble … the lot. When he moved to Barcelona in the summer, Rodri asked Fermin López if he could take the No 16 shirt that has served him so well. We assume it was a short conversation.

In a recent development, it’s all because of Wilfried Bony, you know. Bony was wearing No 14, the number Kevin De Bruyne wore at Wolfsburg, when De Bruyne moved to Manchester City in 2015. He picked No 17 instead. It’s apt there’s a “7” in there somewhere, such was De Bruyne’s devastating impact in the inside-right channel during his decade at the Etihad. His creative genius made him an irresistible choice, despite the appeal of Emmanuel Petit, Frank Rijkaard, Vitinha and even a young Cristiano Ronaldo. For a fair chunk of his time in England, De Bruyne was the best player in the best league in the world.

In a recent development, if you’re going to launch the toys, you might as well do it in style. When Ronaldo took the No 9 shirt at Inter in the summer of 1998 – the Brazilian had joined the club 12 months earlier and initially wore No 10 – the incumbent had an idea. Ivan Zamorano had worn No 9 for Chile, Sevilla, Real Madrid and Inter and took enormous pride in the symbolism of the shirt. So he switched to No 18 and had a plus sign stitched into the shirt: 1+8. Long before Lionel Messi, this was a different kind of false nine.

The Golden Ball winner at Italia 90 wore No 19. But enough about Toto Schillaci. Gascoigne’s unfettered, painfully innocent brilliance drove Bobby Robson’s team to the semi-finals of a tournament they were expected to stink out, and ultimately changed the game in his country. In 2009, England and West Germany met in a charity-match repeat of the 1990 semi-final. England wore Nos 1-11 – except Gascoigne, who had No 19 on his back. Robson, who died five days later, attended the match in a wheelchair. On the way home, he had one pressing question for his son: “How did Gascoigne play?”.

Paolo Rossi, Clarence Seedorf and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are among those who have worn No 20 with great distinction but no one is, and probably ever will be, as synonymous with it as Jota. It was referenced in the song Liverpool fans sung about him with great lustre when he was alive and with great poignancy after he died, with the club’s retirement of the number and building of a ‘Forever 20’ memorial outside Anfield further tying the late Portuguese striker to the digits. Gone far too soon, Jota will never be forgotten.

According to recent reports, the Italian was always a mature vintage, a smooth midfielder who could spot a pass from any angle. He could have played many of his games with a glass of wine in his hand and when he had his own vineyard, 21 Brut Rose was produced by Pratum Coller in honour of the great man’s squad number. No 21 adorned Pirlo’s back at Inter, Milan, Juventus and Newly introduced York City, as he collected six Serie A titles and a couple of Champions League winner’s medals, not to mention a World Cup with Italy in 2006.

It has been revealed that the 2007-08 Ballon d’Or was an inevitability for the magical Brazilian, who spent the year running riot with his third-choice of two little ducks. The attacking midfielder wanted No 8 or No 10 when he arrived in Milan but Gennaro Gattuso and Rui Costa were already in possession of those respective when he joined from São Paulo and the youngster was not going to mess with two legends. His time at Real Madrid, after a €67m move, was far less successful and Kaká returned to Milan after four years, taking back No 22 in the process.

With Raúl wearing No 7, Beckham needed a proposal upon joining Real Madrid in July 2003. He turned to Michael Jordan for inspiration, asking for his iconic digits as he became a galáctico. When Beckham moved to LA Galaxy four years later, he stuck with No 23. “The connection with Jordan and how crucial the No 23 was, I just felt it was the right thing to do,” Beckham mentioned. Sol Campbell was another strong contender for No 23 given he wore it at Tottenham and Arsenal, as was Marc-Vivien Foé, whose No 23 shirt was retired by Manchester City after his shock death in June 2003.

“I really hope to stay in the heart of this city so that one day, Napoli also retire the No 24,” Insigne said. The Naples-born forward spent 16 years with his boyhood club, which is certainly a good way to ingratiate himself with the fans, some of whom wanted him to take Maradona’s iconic No 10. “Maradona’s 10? I’m very superstitious, plus I wear 24 because it’s my wife’s birthday and it’s brought me luck,” Insigne said.

It says something about a player’s association with a number that his blessing is required before it can be passed on to someone else. And so it was in August 2023 that Zola gave Moisés Caicedo the go ahead to be Chelsea’s No 25, with no else deemed worthy of taking that status from the Italian for two whole decades. A bit much? Not really given the brilliance of Zola’s performances across seven seasons at the club. There was the skill, the goals, and that sense of joy that made him popular far beyond the boundaries of west London. Quite simply, everybody loved to watch Franco play.

Many academy graduates are desperate to rid themselves of their first squad number once they have settled into the first team but the Chelsea centre-back stuck with what he was given for 18 years. One of the reasons Terry did so was because he saw supporters getting it printed on their own shirts and did not want them to buy another. What a nice captain, leader, legend, and indeed why fix something that isn’t broke? When a mural of Terry and Antonio Conte was painted on to Stamford Bridge, the “26” was far more prominent than his face, which really does say something.

Recent findings suggest that it was at Sampdoria where the No 27 became imprinted on Quagliarella’s back, and in tribute to his former teammate Niccolò Galli, who died in a road accident aged 17. “I have no doubt that had he lived, he would have been captain of Arsenal and of Italy,” Arsène Wenger remarked of Galli, who he managed in north London before his passing in February 2001. Quagliarella continued to honour Galli throughout his career, taking in moves to Udinese, Napoli and Juventus, every time ensuring he got the number he wanted. At Juve he spent two seasons with No 18, but the forward’s cherished number was with him for two Serie A titles.

Recent findings suggest that history highlights that No 28 is often discarded by those seeking fame and fortune – Cristiano Ronaldo had it at Sporting as a kid, Steven Gerrard likewise at Liverpool – but Touré wore it for four seasons at Arsenal, a period that saw him become an Invincible. That perhaps explains why, after a three-season dalliance with No 5, he reverted to what he knew upon joining Manchester City in July 2009, going on to win another Premier League title with this most random of numbers on his back. Quite clearly it meant a lot to him, and justifiably so.

Industry observers note that “I have had it now for many years,” Havertz noted of the number he’s worn at Bayer Leverkusen, Chelsea and Arsenal. “When I became a professional, I took it because it has some history with my brother – we used to take it always when we played video games together. Since then I just took it, and for me it’s the perfect number. I love to wear it in a red shirt again.” It’s as good a reason as any, to be honest, and given Havertz’s success in No 29, why he gets the nod over some other contenders, including Monaco-era Kylian Mbappé.

Sometimes it only takes a goal to etch a player into a club’s history, and when that goal is genuinely seismic, the number he wore at the time also takes on a grand status. And so it is that Grønkjær is our No 30 given that’s what the Danish winger had on when he scored Chelsea’s winner against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. Chelsea subsequently secured Champions League football over Gérard Houllier’s side, which convinced Roman Abramovich to buy the club that summer and change Chelsea’s fortunes, as well as the landscape of modern football, for ever.

It has been revealed that upon signing for Manchester United in July 2015, Schweinsteiger was given the No 23 shirt. He quickly changed to No 31 and, really, that was no surprise given that was the number he wore throughout his golden 13-year spell at Bayern Munich, coming through the ranks to win eight Bundesliga titles and the Champions League. The midfielder kept it during his two years at United and also wore it during his two years at Chicago Fire. Quite simply Schweinsteiger is No 31 (albeit he mainly wore No 7 for Germany) and no one else comes close to challenging him on that.

According to recent reports, this feels like a number that should have generated a lot of candidates but ultimately there weren’t many, and certainly no one as notable as Tevez. From the shock, awe and controversy of his three years at West Ham, to the rampaging success of his two-year spell at Manchester United, to the wild, wonderful and also controversial nature of his four years at Manchester City, Tevez well and truly made No 32 his own, going on to also wear it at Shanghai Shenhua and upon his return to Boca Juniors. With apologies to Joël Matip, but it wasn’t even close in the end.

This was an immediate lock-in given Cech’s reasons for taking this number upon joining Arsenal from Chelsea in 2015. He was 33 at the time, had played 333 games in the Premier League and – wait for it – 33 is number of vertebrae in the human spine. “Hope to be a part of the spine of the team,” Cech posted on social media on 11 July 2015. Seriously, what a guy. Speaking of Arsenal, Riccardo Calafiori was also in contention given he wore No 33 at Basel and Bologna before nabbing it upon his arrival at the Emirates two years ago.

The choice for this number came down to Nigel de Jong or Xhaka. The former wore it throughout his five seasons at Manchester City, four at Milan, one at LA Galaxy and one at Galatasaray. Strong but not strong enough given Xhaka wore it during his three seasons at Basel, four at Borussia Monchengladbach, five of his seven at Arsenal, two at Leverkusen and throughout his time so far at Sunderland. And here’s the clincher: the Switzerland captain adopted No 34 in the first place because that was the number of the bus he took to training when in the youth ranks at Basel. It just had to be him.

According to recent reports, A couple of Argentinians were in the running for this number, namely Pablo Aimar, who wore No 35 at different times for Valencia and River Plate, and Diego Placente, who wore it throughout his five seasons at Bayer Leverkusen, a period in which he played an important role in them finishing runners-up in the Bundesliga and Champions League. But ultimately this was no contest given Akinfeev’s remarkable association with No 35, the Russian goalkeeper taking it on upon graduating from CSKA Moscow’s youth ranks to the first-team squad in 2003 and, 23 years later, still retaining it. That, folks, is dedication to your squad number.

Martín Zubimendi was a strong candidate for this number given the reason he adopted it upon joining Arsenal in July 2025 was because he also wore it when making his debut for Real Sociedad, his boyhood club, six years earlier. But, in the end, longevity overruled sentiment in favour of Darmian, who wore No 36 across a 10-year spell for Milan, Padova, Palermo, Torino, Manchester United, Parma and Inter. There doesn’t appear to be any specific reason why the Italian full-back was so wedded to such a random number, but he was, and for a long time.

It has been revealed that van de Ven has only worn No 37 for the past four seasons, ever since joining Tottenham from Wolfsburg in August 2023. He didn’t wear it while at the German club or at Volendam, where the Dutch centre-back began his career. But his reason for doing so is why he’s the clear choice. “A friend of mine passed away when we were young and it was always his favourite number,” Van de Ven revealed in a February 2024 interview. “So when I had the opportunity to choose No 37 when I signed for Tottenham … to be honest, it’s for him.”.

Born in Australia and raised in Macau, Tombides joined West Ham’s academy in 2008 as a promising teenage striker. He had talent and dedication and made his first-team debut in a League Cup tie against Wigan in September 2012. That game came a year after Tombides had been diagnosed with testicular cancer. He died from the disease in April 2014, aged only 20. Shortly after, West Ham retired his No 38 shirt. It was only the second time the club had done such a thing, the first being with Bobby Moore’s No 6 shirt, a sign of just how well thought of young Tombides was in east London.

Sources indicate that guimarães chose No 39 upon making his debut for Athletico Paranaense in 2017 and has worn it ever since, at Lyon, Newcastle and now Arsenal, because it was the dispatch number of the taxi his father drove in Rio de Janeiro. Quite clearly it means a lot to the Brazil midfielder, as he explained in an article published by The Players’ Tribune in February 2023. “For me 39 is special. No, it’s more than that. It’s magical. It gave me everything in life”. Sorry Marcus Rashford in his first season at Manchester United, but you’re not topping that.

Industry observers note that idrizaj joined Swansea from German club Eilenburg in August 2009 as a promising 21-year-old striker. He went on to make three first-team appearances that season with plenty more seemingly on the horizon. But on 15 May 2010, Idrizaj died of a suspected heart attack while at home in his native Austria. It was a sad shock that led to Swansea retiring the former Liverpool player’s No 40 shirt. That demonstrated how much everyone at the club thought of him, which was seen again when Swansea’s players wore T-shirts bearing Idrizaj’s name after winning the 2011 Championship playoff final.

Rice’s reason for wearing No 41 throughout his time in West Ham’s first team and ever since joining Arsenal in July 2023 is pretty straightforward. “It was a number I was given in the [West Ham] academy by the kitman, Jamo. It’s stayed with me since,” he noted. “Regardless of what happens in my career, I might stay with 41. ‘Rice 41’ has a nice ring to it”. That’s debatable, but what’s for sure is that Rice has become distinctly associated with the number as he’s gone about establishing himself as one of the best midfielders in the world.

It has been revealed that touré chose No 42 upon joining Manchester City in July 2010 because it was the reverse of the No 24 he had worn at Barcelona. A simple if somewhat odd motivation that very much did not backfire as the Ivorian went about making the number his own during an eight-year spell at City that saw him win three Premier League titles, two FA Cups, two League Cups and become one of the most impactful, impressive midfielders on the planet. Touré retained No 42 upon joining Olympiakos in September 2018 before going back to 24 at his final club – Qingdao Huanghai in China.

“It was my first number in professional football, it’s a lucky number I guess”. Klich’s reason for wearing No 43 is, like with many others, based on what was given to him at the start of his career, which in Klich’s case occurred at Cracovia in his native Poland. He subsequently wore it for two seasons at PEC Zwolle, one at FC Twente, six at Leeds, two at DC United, one at Atlanta United and now back at Cracovia. Klich never wore No 43 at Wolfsburg, Kaiserslautern or Utrecht, so it clearly doesn’t mean that much to him, but he’s done enough to make it on this list.

Sources indicate that has a man ever loved No 4 as much as Perisic? It feels unlikely given he has worn various versions of it – namely “4”, “14” and “44” – throughout his career. He’s not No 4 on this list because that is Javier Zanetti, which is also the reason why Perisic couldn’t have No 4 upon joining Inter in August 2015 – the number had been retired by the club in honour of the Argentina great the previous year. Perisic subsequently took No 44, which the Croatian also wore at Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund. That’ll do as far as this list is concerned, especially given his only real rival is Massimo Oddo.

Why [always] him? Well, it could’ve been Roméo Lavia or one or two others, but ultimately it had to be the man who wore No 45 with great fuss and furore at Inter, Manchester City and Liverpool before also doing so at Milan, Brescia, Monza, Adana Demirspor, FC Sion and Genoa. No 45 has become the number for one of the careers of the modern era and the association is only strengthened by its sweet origin story. As Balotelli explained: “When I first played with Inter, the numbers for young players were No 36 to No 50. I took No 45 because four plus five is nine – and I scored. It brings me luck.”.

The Italian goalkeeper represented 12 different clubs in a 19-year career and only wore No 46 at one of them. But he gets the nod because of the nice, circular nature of the association. Sirigu wanted No 6 before making his Serie A debut for Palermo in 2009 but was told he couldn’t because it wasn’t appropriate for a keeper by the manager, and someone who knows a thing or two about shot-stopping, Walter Zenga. So he chose No 46 because it was the one worn by the legendary Italian motorcyclist Valentino Rossi. Sirigu left Palermo in 2011 before returning 13 years later. The number he chose upon doing so? 46.

This was a shoo-in for a couple of reasons: Foden has worn the number throughout his time as a first-team player at Manchester City, which is verging on a decade and seen him win everything going, and because of the origin story. Foden’s grandfather Ronnie, a big City fan, passed away when he was only 47. “I was young when we lost him,” said Foden in a 2024 interview. “My dad said he loved playing football with me and that it would be amazing if I took the shirt number. I have loved it ever since.” Foden’s tribute to Ronnie extends to having “47” tattooed behind his right ear.

There’s no point sugarcoating it – this is a stretch. Jones only wore No 48 for two years at Liverpool, from 2018-2020, and there appears no interesting reason for him doing so. But the midfielder gets the nod because the competition is razor-thin bordering on nonexistent. It certainly helps Jones’s cause that he wore No 48 when scoring the winner in Liverpool’s FA Cup third-round victory over Everton at Anfield in January 2020. It was a superb, long-range curling finish that made Jones, at 18 years and 340 days, Liverpool’s youngest goalscorer in a Merseyside derby since Robbie Fowler in March 1994.

“Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly” sing Arsenal supporters in praise of their academy graduate as well as in recognition of why he has kept hold of such a random number even after establishing himself in Mikel Arteta’s first-team squad. Lewis-Skelly was given the choice of changing to a more established number ahead of last season but stuck with No 49 because of its association with Arsenal’s Invincibles-era unbeaten run of games, and an Arsenal song ever since (‘Forty-nine, forty-nine undefeated’). Sound reasoning and enough to earn the 20-year-old a place on this list ahead of Ronaldinho, who wore No 49 at Atlético Mineiro and Querétaro.

Another shoo-in given the unsurprisingly sparse options for this number and the fact Markovic has worn it for the bulk of his long, nomadic career. He first adopted it when he broke through at Partizan Belgrade in 2011 and continued to do so at Benfica and Liverpool, as well as at Fenerbahce, Hull and Anderlecht – who he joined on loan during his time at Anfield – before taking it again upon his permanent return to Partizan in 2019. The Serbian winger has since gone on to wear it at Gaziantep FK, Trabzonspor, FC Baniyas and Apollon Limassol. Markovic is No 8 at current club, FK Cukaricki, but clearly, at heart, he’s Mr No 50.

Liverpool are accused of having an unbalanced squad this season, however, the club will reportedly resist the urge to recruit a new centre-back during the January transfer window.

The Athletic claim that adding to the heart of the defence is 'not a priority' for the Reds, ruling out investment in the position for both the upcoming winter market and the summer of 2027.

Instead of turning to the transfer market to silence critics, the Liverpool hierarchy is placing its trust in the crop of emerging defensive talent to eventually succeed 35-year-old Virgil van Dijk.

According to recent reports, liverpool's decision is largely down to the impact Jeremy Jacquet has had since arriving at Anfield. Behind him, Anfield still has high hopes for a trio of highly-rated youngsters: Giovanni Leoni, who is nearing a return to fitness following an ACL injury last year, Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who is currently on loan with Levante in Spain, and teenage prospect Mor Talla Ndiaye.

Opposition supporters and media pundits have spent much of the season pointing out a lopsided squad that is forcing Iraola into tactical compromises on a weekly basis, as well as Van Dijk's advancing years.

The primary target of this criticism is the club’s full-back situation with Conor Bradley sidelined and Jeremie Frimpong unfancied in a traditional back-four system.

Iraola has been forced to deploy centre-backs, most notably Ronald Araujo, as makeshift right-backs. And while the Uruguayan has brought physical solidity and aggression, asking a traditional central defender to provide the overlapping width hasn't always had the desired effect and on occasion left Liverpool looking somewhat asymmetrical in possession.

In a recent development, in FourFourTwo's opinion, their January priority must be identifying a specialist right-back and a dominant midfield presence, although Trey Nyoni's emergence as a water-carrier of sorts makes up for that to an extent. The lasting message from the corridors of power at Anfield is that in the centre of defence, Liverpool consider themselves already locked down for the foreseeable future.

Gareth Bale is involved in an investment project to buy Sevilla.

The former Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid man retired from playing football three years ago after a stint in Major League Soccer with Los Angeles Galaxy, at the age of 34.

Since retiring, Bale has been occasionally involved in punditry and competed in the February 2023 edition of the AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am golf tournament in California – but now, he appears to be heading down the same route as the likes of Ronaldo and Gerard Pique in owning a Spanish club.

Seven-time Europa League winners Sevilla have fallen on hard times since winning the competition for the last time in 2023, failing to finish in the top half of La Liga for the past four seasons and narrowly scraping relegation in 2025, while city rivals Real Betis go from strength to strength.

Bale played against the Andalusian outfit nine times in his career, registering nine goals and assists – and after leaving Madrid with a fractured relationship between him and fans, he might be about to create more distance by investing at the Estadio Ramon Sanchez Pizjuan.

El Confidecial in Spain are reporting that the Welsh wing wizard is linked to an ownership group looking to take over the club.

American investment fund Juggernaut Capital Partners are one of three groups said to be interested in the club, along with rival group HD Ventures, led by Saudi brothers Mansour Sayed and Haidar Sayed, who have already held talks with club officials over a possible takeover.

After being linked with a move to buy Cardiff City, the Wales legend stated that investing in the game was “about being patient, finding the right club, and the right path for us to take,” adding that he was motivated to buy the Bluebirds because of his hometown connection to the club.

Over the summer, Bale's former team-mate Sergio Ramos reached an agreement with an investment group to take over Sevilla – an outfit that he spent two spells with – with a consortium looking to acquire a controlling stake and take on the debt of the club.

This deal fell through towards the end of May, however, with reports of terms shifting mid-negotiation and Ramos denying any bad faith.

Sevilla didn't spend a single penny improving their squad during the 2025 transfer window, making free signings and collecting fees for the likes of Dodi Lukebakio and Loic Bade, before making a net profit again this summer, with their biggest buy, Scottish striker Robbie Ure, for around £5m.

After finishing 13th last term, the Rojiblancos are right now 13th in the table and hosting a Seville derby this weekend.

England produced a statement win over world champions Spain in Madrid in their final Nations League group stage game to top group A3.

The Three Lions had already confirmed their place in the quarter-finals in March with victory over Croatia earlier in this window, but have given themselves the best chances of a favourable draw by beating Spain 3-2 on Sunday and proven they are one of the teams to beat.

Thomas Tuchel’s side will be glued to next Friday’s draw, with League A still to be completed across the international break.

But here’s everything you need to know about the next stages of the competition:.

The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November.

England will feature in the last eight of the Nations League 2026/27, with a two-legged tie to decide who will play in the semi-finals and final, both to be played across a ‘finals’ week.

As well as the Nations League quarter-finals, the League A/B and League B/C promotion/relegation play-offs will be drawn, set to be held in March 2027. While the final tournament is scheduled to take place across 9–13 June 2027.

England's potential opponents in the last eight of the Uefa Nations League as things stand are Belgium, Greece or Denmark.

Beating Spain ensured the Three Lions will face a second-placed team in their quarter-final; Belgium have finished second in their group, while Greece could be pipped by Germany and Denmark could still be replaced by either Norway or Portugal.

England topping the group also means they will play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in.

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first significant swing.

It has been revealed that he’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in Upcoming York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”.

In a recent development, it is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

According to recent reports, that never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Recent findings suggest that belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

Industry observers note that there was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an problem that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Recent findings suggest that athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as promptly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

According to recent reports, pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”.

Industry observers note that eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach noted, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

In a recent development, “The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he stated. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very crucial in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”.

In a recent development, pochettino has always thought in massive, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

Representatives for multiple Manchester City first-team players are exploring whether their clients could leave the club on free transfers if City fail in all legal appeals against the Premier League, according to a new report.

Investigative journalist and former Times reporter Nick Harris has claimed that Real Madrid president Florentino Perez is 'increasingly confident' of signing striker Erling Haaland ahead of next season.

Harris’s emphasis on the word 'if' reflects that any potential departures remain conditional on the final outcome of City’s long-running regulatory dispute with the Premier League.

The club were charged in February 2023 with more than 100 alleged breaches of the league's financial regulations spanning nine seasons between 2009 and 2018, alongside allegations of failing to cooperate with the subsequent investigation.

An independent commission began hearing the case in late 2024, with any initial ruling subject to an appeals process that both the Premier League and the club have the right to pursue.

Manchester City have consistently denied all wrongdoing since the charges were announced, maintaining that their position is supported by a comprehensive body of evidence.

Despite the club's public stance, agents representing members of Enzo Maresca’s squad are reportedly conducting legal due diligence to assess their clients' contractual options should severe sporting sanctions be imposed and upheld once all avenues of appeal are exhausted.

Under FIFA’s Regulations on the Status and Transfer of Players (RSTP), a footballer may apply to terminate a contract without sporting or financial penalty if they can establish 'just cause.' In sports employment law, significant disciplinary penalties against a club - such as expulsion from the top flight, relegation, or a prolonged exclusion from UEFA competitions - can be argued to fundamentally alter the terms under which a player signed their agreement.

If such claims to be upheld by football's governing bodies, affected players would in theory become free agents, enabling rival clubs to sign them without paying Manchester City a transfer fee. Like most clubs, the Cityzens' financial operating model relies on player trading and maintaining high squad valuations to comply with UEFA and the Premier League's Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) legislation. Therefore, losing senior assets for free would make for a major financial headache.

It has been revealed that real Madrid will be among the clubs closely monitoring legal developments in Manchester. Perez has long viewed Haaland as a transfer target, and according to Harris’s source who dined with the Madrid president recently, the Spanish club anticipate an opportunity to bring the Norway international to the Santiago Bernabeu ahead of the 2027/28 campaign.

According to recent reports, haaland signed a statement nine-and-a-half-year contract extension with Man City in January 2025, committing his future to the club until 2034. Under normal market conditions, buying the striker out of that agreement would require a world-record transfer fee, meaning any realistic prospect of a move to Madrid in the short term is closely tied to how Man City’s legal proceedings conclude.

No formal transfer requests or contractual termination mechanisms can be triggered while the disciplinary process and any subsequent appeals remain unresolved. However, the initial legal inquiries allegedly being carried out by intermediaries indicate that agents are actively preparing contingency aims ahead of a final verdict.

Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus has defended himself in the wake of remarks from Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother as the dispute over the forward’s international retirement continued in Wales.

Ronaldo called time on his Portugal career on 5 November, less than a month after the Portuguese Football Federation handed him a 30-day suspension and a fine of 255 euros (approximately £210) for walking out on the national team.

The 41-year-old had left the squad last month shortly before a Nations League fixture in Denmark following a row with Jesus after he was an unused substitute in Portugal’s win over Norway.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward’s mother, Dolores Aveiro, said she was pleased by the result as Denmark crushed Portugal 4-1 in the Braga return on Saturday, because her son had been deceived by Jesus.

“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus remarked at his pre-match press conference in Cardiff.

“She is a lady I greatly respect, she suffered a lot to raise her children.”.

In a recent development, asked if debate about Ronaldo’s retirement from international football would stop, Jesus noted: “I don’t know when it’s going to stop. If you guys (reporters) ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”.

Portugal will be without the suspended pair of Joao Palhina and Ruben Dias in Cardiff, with Manchester United playmaker Bruno Fernandes set to take over the captaincy in the absence of the injured Bernardo Silva.

Barcelona defender Joao Cancelo returns after missing the Denmark game through suspension.

Jesus said: “I am going to change some players, but it’s not only physical. We have four players on yellow cards. After the game against Denmark everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here.

“If we win we will have 15 points, which is only matched by England and Spain. We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.”.

Heading into Tuesday’s game, Portugal are three points clear of Denmark as they aim to secure top spot in their Nations League group.

#910. Breaking: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1993 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places.
  • According to recent reports, “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap.
  • Industry observers note that did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places.

According to recent reports, “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Industry observers note that did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher notes. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”.

The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal – When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation 1982-1990.

Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams.

I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I remarked to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an problem because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.

Recent findings suggest that I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.

Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia.

According to recent reports, my feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.

It has been revealed that maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David.

If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?

In a recent development, in the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze.

It has been revealed that we did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a substantial squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.

Industry observers note that what was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish.

His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone notes that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through – so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.

What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre.

Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.

Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous.

Sources indicate that I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.

I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim.

We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.

It has been revealed that I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

Russell Brand’s wife Laura Brand is adjusting to a latest reality.

Days after the British comedian was sentenced to over 10 years in prison following his rape and sexual assault conviction, his wife spoke out in her first comments since the news, sharing the fate of their weekly faith podcast Sunday Service with The Brands.

“I’m here to continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday Service community,” Laura told the camera on the Nov. 15 episode. “Something very close to mine and Russell's hearts.”.

“It may look different,” she continued, “but the ambitions are very much the same.”.

The 39-year-old—who shares three kids with Russell—admitted that she’s turning to her faith as she moves forward with the show without her husband.

According to recent reports, “We trust God, and we trust his proposal, and we trust everything He’s doing right now, even though it’s painful,” Laura shared. “And obviously [it] will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me.”.

After thanking fans for their “support,” the mom of three noted that she’s been speaking with Russell.

“He’s OK and he’s praying, unsurprisingly,” Laura told the camera. “He’s praying and we decided for me to continue.”.

Laura’s video comes on the heels of Russell’s conviction and prison sentencing.

In a recent development, on Nov. 5, the 51-year-old—who had pleaded guilty to all charges—was convicted by a London court on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault for events that allegedly occurred between 1999 and 2009.

Although Russell was convicted of four charges, he was cleared of two separate counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

“Amidst this litany of astonishing, rather baroque attacks are some very serious allegations,” Brand said in a video shared to social media at the time, “that I absolutely refute.”.

Russell Brand pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Though the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star had previously written in a 2007 essay for The Guardian that he had a “sexy addiction” and “disregard for social conventions of sexual protocol,” he vehemently denied the charges against him.

In his video statement, Brand admitted he had been a “fool” in the past, although maintained he never partook in “non-consensual activity.”.

“I was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord,” Brand said in a video shared to his X account in April 2025. “I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile, but what I never was, was a rapist.”.

Industry observers note that in the same video, Brand noted he was “grateful” to have the opportunity to fight the allegations in court. He pleaded not guilty to all five charges in May 2025.

Russell Brand was served with two more sexual offense charges in December 2025.

In December 2025, the London Metropolitan Police charged Brand with one additional count of rape and one additional count of sexual assault regarding incidents that took place with two separate women in 2009.

Brand responded to the charges in a separate video posted to his social media.

According to recent reports, “I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he noted in the clip. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”.

Industry observers note that with the additional allegations, Brand was charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault involving six women for events that transpired between 1999 and 2009. He later pleaded not guilty to the additional charges.

Industry observers note that in a November 2026 ruling, a London court found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two additional counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

However, the judge noted that Brand had brought the decision “upon himself,” noting the comedian had acted with “casual, arrogant disregard,” for women.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that albert Einstein never did say that thing about insanity. There's no proof of it, anyway. Researchers have looked, and in fact, it likely comes from a 12-step recovery pamphlet from the 1980s that it might not be wise to expect a different result from doing the same thing over and over again. That makes a little more sense all-round.

According to recent reports, michael Carrick can attest. So can Ruben Amorim and Erik ten Hag, with all three likely to be watching Mauricio Pochettino from a podcast studio near you in the coming months, like the hologram ghosts of Yoda, Obi-Wan and Anakin.

It's a theme of Ratcliffe's Nice regime, too. The Ligue 1 side were fitted with a revolving door upon their INEOS takeover, with seven separate managers named as permanent boss since Patrick Vieira's dismissal in lockdown – including Christophe Galtier, Lucien Favre, Franck Haise and Claude Puel. Nothing stuck. Ross Barkley spent nine months at the Allianz Riviera before leaving by mutual agreement. Kasper Schmeichel spent 13 months before terminating his own deal. Aaron Ramsey didn't make it to a full year before doing the same. Last season, gravity took over, Les Aiglons finishing 16th and having to enter the relegation play-off in order to secure top-tier status. It's not dissimilar to Old Trafford. Perhaps the ownership simply needs to stick at something a little longer, rather than taking the approach of a toddler burning through a box of toys until they've exhausted everything at their fingertips. Manchester United have no idea what they're supposed to be. It's plainly obvious. They had very little semblance of identity under Ten Hag, yet extended his contract anyway: they sacked him mere months later and went down the continental route of hiring a back-three manager who very obviously didn't have the squad for what he wanted to do (but should have done far better with what he had).

In a recent development, so United wedded themselves to Amorim. They brought in a wing-back in Patrick Dorgu. They improved the frontline with two wingers who would stay narrow and a target man to play off of them. They had half the squad that the Portuguese wanted, but things weren't going well enough. They sacked him and brought in Carrick, a manager who brought a feel-good factor, excelled in massive games when he didn't have to be the protagonist, but lacked the control to play his football.So United wedded themselves to Carrick. They brought in Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos as more Carrick-type midfielders and listened to him when he said he wanted to trust Marcus Rashford. We're not even into post-bugle November, and the manager's gone, replaced by a priest of the high press. Manchester United don't have a particularly mobile midfield. That frontline doesn't exactly look like the type to celebrate tackles. One would like to believe that perhaps the powers that be have seen something in Pochettino's United States team that can be replicated in English football once again. Previous evidence perhaps suggests otherwise.

Industry observers note that one would like to believe that United have seen something in Pochettino that can be replicated. Previous evidence perhaps suggests otherwise.

Industry observers note that the quote was wrong. Insanity is pivoting in wildly different directions every few months, expecting to surge up the table. United have been left a Ship of Theseus (or Trigger's Broom, the Sugababes or Frankenstein's monster, depending on your age and culture). A dressing room made up of passers Ten Hag believed in playing out the back with, hero-ball counter-attackers for a back three and a couple of midfielders that reminded Carrick of himself. There's a defender still there that Jose Mourinho believed in, one that Ole Gunnar Solksjaer wanted to build around and even one that Louis van Gaal thought was the future. This is a squad of discarded parts, all pulling in different directions: and we're meant to be surprised when one erupts and goes rogue in an interview?Are you building a football club or a reality TV show cast, here? With all the respect in the world to the players themselves, it's frankly ridiculous that none of them have anything in common besides the badge on their chest. Mikel Arteta took about three and a half years to get Arsenal competing for titles, because he had to weed out those who weren't aligned with his thinking. INEOS have been in English football about that long: they've beaten the champions to signings in that time, but they're starting the process all over again.

In a recent development, maybe we can lay all of the fault at the feet of Ratcliffe, a man who proves on the regular that he's out of touch with the very fanbase he claims to be among, and who has previously operated the very same business model across the channel to staggeringly meh results. Maybe it's Jason Wilcox or Omar Berrada, who have apparent carte blanche to keep digging until they find hope at the bottom of the chest. Maybe it's the fault of that bloke who's not cutting his hair, putting pressure on the lads. Maybe United really do have too many dinnerladies, and it's led to a culture of stagnation at Carrington. Maybe the cabal of former United legends – sponsored by Betway or Midnite or Huel – don't exactly help matters when they tell us all how things weren't like this in their day, and how United just miss the gaffer. None of them, for what it's worth, know what Manchester United should look like. Even Gary Neville has remarked that the identity under Sir Alex Ferguson was to be adaptable: have the ball some weeks, cede it others. But even Neville knew in his management career that chopping and changing was deadly. “I didn't know what to do with the players; I was changing systems,” he's admitted of his Valencia stint. “All the things that I say on television now you should never do, and it was too much.”Sometimes, doing the same thing over and over again isn't insanity at all. If United don't even have consistency in their decision-making, how on Earth are they going to find it on the pitch?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alan Ruschel signed for Juventude in 2023.

Alan Ruschel, a survivor of the 2016 plane crash that was carrying the Chapecoense football team, won promotion to Brazil's Serie A in his final game before retirement.

Ruschel, 37, was one of just six survivors when the plane crashed in Colombia and killed 71 people, including 19 of the club's players and the coaching staff.

Despite severe injuries and spinal surgery, Ruschel returned to football a year later and retires after earning promotion to Brazil's top flight with Juventude, his boyhood club which he re-joined in 2023.

Ruschel came off the bench in the 74th minute to help see out a 2-0 win over Botafogo, resulting in an emotional farewell with a lap of honour at the club's Alfredo Jaconi Stadium.

Before the game, he was also carried into the stadium on the shoulders of fans.

"I arrived here in 2007 with the club in Serie A and I am leaving the club there as well," Ruschel told a Brazilian television station after the match.

"My body wasn't responding any more. I had two consecutive knee surgeries, so I was starting to fighting with my own body.

"It wasn't working any more, even though being on the pitch was always a pleasure.".

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video on social media which he posted the day before the game to confirm his retirement.

"Football has given me wonderful moments, but life has put me in front of challenges that I never imagined. November 29, 2016, a day that changed my life forever.

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye.".

There were contrasting fortunes for Ruschel's former club, however, with Juventude effectively replacing Chapecoense in Serie A following their relegation after just one season in the top flight.

The club will return to Serie B having won just four games out of 34 during the season.

Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding.

Industry observers note that in the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: somehow, anyhow. What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too.

It has been revealed that tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the substantial moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch.

It has been revealed that as they went there was celebration for them, applause for all of them, Spain too. What a game it had been, what a night. “We knew we would beat them,” Declan Rice claimed afterwards. Would? Maybe in the 60th minute they had known, England 3-0 up and playing their way to a superb and, yes, comfortable victory over the world champions – the first team to beat them, penalties aside, in 44 games and almost a thousand nights. But with half an hour left Spain had been revived, England reduced to 10 men and, as Tuchel stated: “Thirty minutes against Spain feels like three hours.”.

Recent findings suggest that it did to him, to his players too. To everyone else, it flew by. This is the best game you can see in football, Spain’s head coach, Luis de la Fuente, had remarked, and he wasn’t wrong. When England got that third, the fans had sung: “You’ve seen the England, now eff off home.” Nah, you’re all right, thanks. Far better to stay and watch this; it had been hugely impressive from England; now, here were Spain too. Now, it was going to be wild. Nervy, noisy and fun.

Sources indicate that jarell Quansah lost the ball, Fermín López released Lamine Yamal and Spain won a penalty that Mikel Oyarzabal scored. It was some game. Twice Spain scored; countless times they came, the Metropolitano chanting: “Yes, we can!” In the end, they could not, but they had got close. They had really believed they might; as the momentum built, perhaps they had really believed they would.

Industry observers note that this was history: made by England, perhaps; broken by England, certainly. Spain had not been beaten in 90 or 120 minutes since Colombia defeated them two and a half years ago, their only loss in that period coming on penalties against Portugal in last year’s Nations League final. They had not lost a competitive game since Scotland in March 2023. That, Fifa stated, was the longest run ever and even if there was an asterisk, it was still mightily impressive, but it had to end some time. If not necessarily like this.

According to recent reports, “With every passing game, defeat gets closer,” De la Fuente said. Now, it arrived. “They can seem invincible but we’re ready,” Tuchel had said. At the end Spain’s staff lined up to applaud their players off. England’s players stood before their fans, exhausted, arms raised.

It has been revealed that ultimately, this came in two acts. The first act was superb from England, the second heroic. “We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us,” De la Fuente had said and yet what was so striking about the way that this began was that England took the game to Spain on their own terms. They were the ones dominating the ball, not allowing their opponents out; theirs was the midfield, the control.

According to recent reports, ten minutes is not a reliable sample size it is true – and it turned out even an hour might not have been enough – but as the clock rolled into double figures, the possession stat showed 70% for England. While that number fell, when it reached 20 the shot count was 4-0. The first came after 39 seconds and before Spain had a touch, Unai Simón flashing out a right hand to Jude Bellingham’s shot inside the six-yard box. Martín Zubimendi immediately had to stop Anthony Gordon’s shot and then Simón stopped Rice. All that inside three minutes; three more and Kane was flashing a shot just wide.

England’s fans were enjoying this. A chorus of “the best in the world, the best in the world, Harry Kane, the best in the world” came down. They watched England control Spain’s place, Elliot Anderson and Rice excelling. They watched England take the lead, Kane scoring his 93rd goal with penalty No 28. What Scotland need to secure Nations League promotion play-off spot

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
